#3652. Even the PS5 Pro is "not powerful enough" to run GTA 6 at 60FPS or 40FPS, Rockstar says

Don't expect GTA 6 to get an update supporting higher framerate modes, at least, not on current-generation consoles. Rockstar has explained that even the most powerful console of the bunch, the PS5 Pro, isn't powerful enough to run the lavish game at 40FPS or 60FPS.

Last week, some players weren't too happy with the news that GTA 6 is targeting 30FPS on all platforms it's currently launching on - PS5 Pro, PS5, Xbox Series X and Xbox Series S. Like countless other big productions this generation, the hope was that Rockstar Games would offer both quality and performance modes for its lush open-world monster.

Rockstar's now seemingly confirmed that its crime epic won't run at 60FPS or 40FPS anytime soon, simply because it can't on the currently available hardware.

"While the PS5 Pro's central processor is slightly better than the PS5 base console, it is not powerful enough to run the game's complex simulation at higher frame rates," the studio's technology production director, Marc Chambers, said in a statement to Kotaku. There you have it, then - even the beefiest console around can't handle Leonida at higher framerates.

Chambers did note some of the souped up console's other technical improvements, however: "Our base presentation makes use of ray-traced reflections and global illumination. On the PS5 Pro, this is enhanced with the addition of ray-traced shadows, as well as overall added clarity through the use of PlayStation Spectral Super Resolution (PSSR). The PS5 Pro features an upgraded graphics processor and upscaling technology that we leverage to increase the game's visual fidelity."

The tech gurus over at Digital Foundry gave some more insight into how GTA 6 runs on current-gen machines, calling it a "technical tour de force," though one that can still dip below 30FPS on PS5 and Xbox Series X during busier chase scenes and explosive shootouts. It's perhaps unsurprising, then, that higher framerates are off the table for now.

A 30FPS launch is by no means a departure for Rockstar Games, either. GTA 5 also ran at an unsteady 30FPS when it first dropped onto the Xbox 360 and PS3, with 60FPS support only coming alongside the game's PC port more than a year later. I'm not too fussed about the game's 30FPS target, personally. I'd much rather have a game that consistently hits 30FPS than one that continuously chugs trying to reach 60FPS, especially when it's as frequently drop dead gorgeous as GTA 6.

The slightly lower framerates haven't affected the game's critical response so far, either. In Eurogamer's GTA 6 review, our Chris Tapsell called it a "game of opposites and awe, minute detail and impossible scale" as "Rockstar pushes back the horizon of video games once again."

If you're planning to jump into the game at midnight - or if you're virtually travelling to New Zealand for early entry - there's a few things to be aware of. First is that you won't be able to replay GTA 6's missions without multiple save files, so be sure to soak it all up. Second, some Ultimate Edition content is only available in the first chapter.

Rockstar's budget doesn't "represent a business model anyone else can or probably should emulate"

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

It's pretty much impossible to describe GTA 6 as anything other than a massive success. It is expected to break commercial records set by GTA 5 and it's tied with only The Legend of Zelda: Ocarina of Time as the highest rated game of all time on Metacritic. And yet, because we're living in 2026 after all, many Rockstar developers who helped bring the game to life are now worrying about losing their jobs.

Writing for The Guardian, Rockstar animation programmer Nestor Uriart argues in support of this month's UK-wide Rockstar Games union-recognition ballot, believing unionization is key to "safeguard our jobs."

Games like Battlefield 6, and the layoffs that happened after its commercially successful launch, prove time and time again that strong sales and reviews are nothing compared to shareholder value when it comes to deciding whether or not to implement mass layoffs at a studio backed by a publicly traded company. And yet, you'd think having your name attached to the literal biggest game of all time would get you some sense of job security, but apparently that's not the case for everyone at Rockstar.

"While the highs of a game release like this can be incredible, game workers have also come to expect other, less welcome side effects: intense overtime in the buildup and mass redundancies in the aftermath," writes Uriart, arguing that unionizing could also help address allegations Rockstar has faced in the past of crunch culture. "With a strong union we could make sure there is no return to this system. We have already seen the introduction of some overtime pay, and now we want to keep on pushing to ensure that every hour worked in our industry is an hour paid."

Uriart says there's been "no indication that layoffs are coming, but it’s hard not to worry about what the future holds. Studios across the industry have been slashing huge portions of their workforces, with an estimated 24,000 roles axed globally over the last two years.

"It says a lot about the industry that even my colleagues and I, working on the biggest game of all time, are worried about getting laid off. But the truth is that workers across the sector are helpless to resist the waves of redundancies crashing around us, until we get organised."

As GTA 6 is just releasing this week, it's impossible to get a picture of the scale of its commercial success. We already know it's the most pre-ordered game of all time, but that was almost a given. Perhaps I'm being naive, but I would like to think it's going to be so overwhelmingly successful that Take-Two holds off on making any large-scale staffing changes. That said, now that development is transitioning into post-launch support, it's reasonable as a developer on the team to worry about downsizing.

#3648. GTA 6 won't let you use cheats until you complete the main story, and locks progression when you do

Here's a twist: you can't use cheats in Grand Theft Auto 6 until you complete the entire game's main story.

That's what we discovered from our tests at least, after loading in saves at various points through the game to be sure, and it's also both a first for the series and a departure even from how developer Rockstar handled cheats in Red Dead Redemption 2. In that game,approximately half of the cheats were available from the off, and the other half required discovering specific newspapers from around the game's world to unlock.

In GTA 6, you'll again need to do some legwork. This time it appears that all of the game's cheats not only require you to finish the story, but also complete various tasks or challenges to unlock them.

The way it works is simple enough. Once you finish the main story, the "Cheats" tab - previously hidden - quietly appears at the far end of the Progress menu, accessible when you open the in-game map and scroll with the bumper buttons. From there, you can view various sub-sections of cheats, sorted by category, and a list of 10 or so cheats for each.

With each cheat there'll be a short explanation of what it does, and what's required to unlock it and, once unlocked, guidance on how to perform it. This is done via whipping out your phone, holding down the shoulder buttons and using various D-Pad inputs - much the same as GTA 5.

There's also another caveat to bear in mind: when you use a cheat, you'll see a notification warning you that the game can't be saved while it's active, and that Trophies and Achievements are also disabled until you end that session. This makes sense, once you understand the nature of GTA 6's story - there is a cheat for giving yourself a load of money, for instance; another departure from GTA 5 where that popular cheat was removed - but given you'll need certain amounts of cash at various points of the story, enabling you to shortcut that would disrupt the way the narrative unfolds.

We'll have a guide from yours truly to all the game's cheats live on Eurogamer in the very near future, as the game releases here in the UK. In the meantime, if you find yourself on the fence about this one, be sure to give our GTA 6 review a look. As I put it there, giving the game five stars: it is "the most believable and unbelievable video game world ever made".

Jennifer Svedberg-Yen says she left the studio in July after finishing up work on the studio's hit RPG.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

Jennifer Svedberg-Yen, lead writer of the hit 2025 RPG Clair Obscur: Expedition 33, has revealed that she is no longer with developer Sandfall Interactive. In an interview with Gamesbeat, Svedberg-Yen said she wants to return to her own creative efforts, including stories for film and television, and also aims to set up a new fund specifically to support the advancement of narrative design in games.

Clair Obscur: Expedition 33 was universally acclaimed and won an astounding list of awards, including just about every narrative-focused prize you can name: Best Storytelling at the Golden Joysticks, Best Narrative at The Game Awards, Outstanding Achievement in Story at DICE, Best Narrative at the GDC Awards, Best Narrative at the BAFTAs, and Hugo and Nebula awards. That makes it particularly interesting that Clair Obscur is Svedberg-Yen's one and only game credit: Prior to joining Sandfall Interactive in 2020 as one of its earliest members, she spent years working in the finance industry.

Despite Clair Obscur's success, Svedberg-Yen revealed that she moved on from the game, and the studio, earlier this year. "I left Sandfall in July, after wrapping up some final stuff for Expedition," she said. "We’ve parted ways."

That has to hurt for Sandfall, but Svedberg-Yen still has ambitions within the game industry, including the creation of an investment fund for "narrative-focused game creators, trying to bridge the gap between the seed stage and going to publishers."

"This is the chicken and egg question a lot of people face," Svedberg-Yen said. "To get money from publishers you need a demo, but to make a demo you need money. To get money you have to go to publishers. That’s an area where I would like to help a lot of these smaller creatives to get that seed funding so they can, in a way, de-risk themselves in the eyes of bigger investors.

"In that way I can also help them build a stronger narrative foundation from the beginning. I’ve done a lot of consulting work with different studios. I’ve discovered that quite a lot of studios don’t really know how to think about narrative, or how to integrate it into their pipelines and their processes. They tend to think it’s a very narrow thing, when in fact it can influence all aspects. Part of this would also be an incubation program to help these studios develop those narrative foundations."

Svedberg-Yen said a lot of studios think of narrative as "a skin," something thrown on near the end of the development process once everything else is assembled. But that's like trying to solve a puzzle without knowing whether there's actually a solution at all, she continued, "whereas if you start from the very beginning, when everyone is starting from the same jumping-off point, everything will naturally be able to tie together."

The goal is not to compete with publishers, she explained, but "to find a way to work with them to get us back on solid ground. Above all, I really would like to champion other people and other creatives to have a chance to pursue their dreams, have a chance to make the games they want to make."

That investment fund, alongside her own projects and stories, will be Svedberg-Yen's primary focus in the coming year: "The strongest feeling in me right now for 2027 is I want to help. That sounds so cheesy and idealistic. I always cringe at myself for saying it. But I don’t know how else to say it and be truthful. I want to help in some way, help the industry."

#3646. Korridor turns those Youtube ads for vertical mobile shooters into a new, "deeply strategic" genre, and I can't decide if it's lying

The electro-metal OST seems legit, at least

I like to think I'm difficult to hypnotise, but I confess, I'm a sucker for those Youtube adverts for the mobile vertical shooters. You know the ones: boglins pour towards an auto-firing player, who must dodge about to grab upgrades while whittling down the horde. The player in the advert always does pretty well for 20 seconds, but ahhhh, then they get just a tiny bit overconfident, mistime how long it'll take them to erode the health of an ogre midboss, and: bam!

Show me one of those ads, and I'll always watch to the end in the hope that this time, the protagonist will Study The Blade, conquer their harmatia, and slay the damn ogre. I've never actually played any of the mobile shooters in question, mind you. I'm far too cultured for that, you dope! Except that I've just been playing the demo for Korridor, which is supposedly "based off" of the ads, but might as well be one of the games they're promoting, for all I know.

Per the Steam page, it claims to have turned the above advert format into a whole new "deeply strategic genre", the "gates shooter", by stirring in "elements of roguelikes and bullet heavens". I need somebody to authenticate whether this is a truthful statement, or developer TinyToad pulling a fast one. In the meantime, I'll say that 1) I have now managed to kill several ogres, 2) I like Korridor's electro-metal soundtrack.

In Korridor, you're a bald medieval monk garbed in Poundshop Adeptus Astartes platemail. You've woken up in a dungeon of mysterious provenance, and must walk very slowly down its corridors korridors while shooting and punching goblins, wraiths and demons hurrying the other way. Each enemy has a numerical health indicator, and the basic challenge is working out whether you can empty it before they walk into you – which costs you a proportionate amount of health, mitigated by armour. As you go, you'll walk through a choice of gates that grant buffs such as faster health regen, bullet penetration, or nippier horizontal motion.

The fact that you don't control how fast the monk trudges vertically allows the game to synch the onslaught pretty tightly to the thudding, growling score. It reminds me a little of Thumper, though it isn't nearly so invigoratingly malevolent. So far. At intervals, the beat thickens and all the enemies burst into a sprint, throwing their arms up and conveying the strong impression that they are more running away from something than running at you. There's clearly a dreadful entity at the far end of the dungeon. Perhaps it is another overdressed monk with an even bigger gun.

Is this how those mobile games actually work? If it is, then alas and alack, all is lost. I've finally succumbed to those adverts, and all it took was some disingenuous Steam copy promising to place them at a critical remove. Curse you, TinyToad. Curse you and your gates. If you were actually a toad, I'd step on you. Still, now that we've broken the ice, can you please make another game in which I get to play one of those gloating giantesses in Hero Wars? Because I know some people who dig that kind of thing.

#3645. Delete GTA 6 from your hard drive and indie publisher Devolver Digital might give you a free game

GTA 6 is out at midnight everywhere (19th November), but it's far from the only game in town. Indie publisher Devolver Digital is taking on the open-world behemoth with its very own Volvy's Adventure: Reslimed, out the same day, and you can win a free copy of the platformer by proving you've deleted GTA 6 off your hard drive.

"Want a free copy of November's hottest release? Repost this tweet with a video of you deleting your GTA6 pre-load along with #MakeRoomForVolvy for a chance to win a copy of Volvy's Adventure: Reslimed on Steam," the publisher wrote on social media.

It's not every day you see a publisher promote its own games by asking folks to delete another company's release, but arguably the wildest part of the giveaway is that Volvy's Adventure isn't launching on consoles. Even if you were to scrub GTA 6's 212GB pre-load from your PS5 or Xbox, you're definitely not making room for Volvy.

"Heads up: Volvy's Adventure: Reslimed is launching exclusively on PC. While we expect to see console GTA deletions in your submissions, Steam keys are the only prize available for this giveaway," Devolver noted.

Devolver made quite an amusing GTA 6 parody trailer, as well, which sees Volvy and Miss Volvy running from the police and getting steamy in the shower. I've embedded it up above for your viewing pleasure.

For the unaware, Volvy used to be a common fixture at Devolver Digital's frequently bonkers notE3 presentations. He's now somewhat of a company mascot. But while Volvy's Adventure: Reslimed is being presented as a "much-anticipated remaster of the original remake of the hit action-platformer," this is, in fact, Volvy's first proper game. Making up an elaborate history for Volvy is just part of the publisher's long-running and increasingly questionable gag.

Gunbrella and Gato Robot developer doinksoft is behind this one, a throwback side-scrolling platformer where our mouse-like mascot uses his oversized hand to helicopter over gaps, punch through roadblocks and, erm, fist himself underground, per the game's Steam page.

Devolver Digital has been waiting to steal Rockstar's thunder for well over a year now. The publisher threatened to release a game on GTA 6's release date way back in May 2025, and has pushed back its plan with each new GTA 6 delay. Gotta respect the commitment, at least.

#3644. 32 Spoiler-Free Tips As You Hop Into Grand Theft Auto 6

Grand Theft Auto 6GTA 6Rockstar GamesTips

Grand Theft Auto 6 is finally here. The long wait was totally worth it. It is one of the best games I’ve played in many years and easily the best Grand Theft Auto game ever made. It is also a big, complicated, and deep game, with so much to do and see.

So, to help you out, here’s a bunch of tips for players hopping into GTA 6 this week. Don’t worry, no spoilers are included below.

Without spoiling anything, there are some incredibly big surprises and really memorable moments buried in this game. I highly recommend that people avoid watching too many videos about GTA 6 ahead of playing it to avoid ruining one particular late-game moment that might be one of my favorite video game surprises in years.

Before you rush out the door to do some missions or rob a liquor store, take a moment to grab a bite and a drink. These items will buff your health, stamina, and focus meter, letting you take more damage, run longer, and slow down time more during combat.

And hey, don’t assume that just because you’re drinking a soda or eating a hot dog, you have to stop moving or shooting. In GTA 6, you can move, shoot, run, hold hands, and even drive while holding and eating food. Finally, you can crack a cold one while shooting a rifle.

Around the map, you’ll encounter dogs and cats. If you hold the left trigger, you can zoom in on them and then praise and pet them. And you should do this, not just because dogs and cats are great, but also because it buffs your focus and rewards you with some good behavior points toward your criminal profile.

In GTA 6, you can store guns and clothes in your personal car’s trunk. And you should do this, as changing clothes is a great and fast way to lose the attention of the police.

You can manage your clothing, create new custom outfits, and store clothes in your trunk at any clothing store with a changing room, so don’t feel like you have to head back home to change your outfits around or remove stuff from your trunk. Just find a store.

Also, Rockstar lets you rename your custom outfits using a list of pre-existing words, like clubbing, hunting, or everyday. I recommend doing that to make it easier at a glance to see what everything stored in your trunk actually is without having to put it on and check.

When you go out shopping for clothesâand you will likely do that because dressing up is so much fun in this gameâbring both Jason and Lucia. This will let you buy clothing for both of them, try on new items as either character, and modify their current attire. And bonus: Buying clothing for your partner gets you some extra romance points.

The world of Leonida is packed with random events and moments that you can encounter while just walking around. These can be as simple as a drug deal going bad, or as complex as someone who needs help finding their missing spouse after a night partying. Often these events will be signaled to the player via shouting or other loud noises. If you hear something like that, click the left and right sticks to activate focus mode and find the source of the commotion, and then go investigate it.

I spent many hours making sure to close it first, then realized it closed when you drive away. You can also hold left on the D-pad to access your car’s features, including the ability to turn off headlights and close (or open) the trunk.

This section of Jason and Lucia’s phone will update as you play and will remind you to call certain characters or reply to texts. This can often reveal new story moments and dialogue between Lucia and Jason and their various friends and criminal cohorts.

Very early into GTA 6, you unlock the ability to explore underwater shipwrecks and find valuable loot. And you should do some of these in the early hours of GTA 6 to earn some easy cash. Plus, it’s just fun to explore the ocean.

On Jason and Lucia’s phones, you’ll find an app called Scooter Bros. This lets you manage your owned vehicles, spawn them near you, and even repair them. However, this isn’t free and early on money will be tight, so be careful how often you rely on this convenient app. It can also get vehicles out of police impound lots, but that ain’t cheap.

It costs $12,500 to upgrade to the premium version of the Scooter Bros service, which, for many hours in the game, is going to be more than you can spare. But once you feel comfortable spending that much, I recommend it. It gives you three free uses of the app every in-game day, which saves money in the long run. Plus, the app is upgraded and says you’re premium, and that’s nice.

Eventually, GTA 6 will let you buy garages around the map. These aren’t very useful while driving about, but they do give you more slots to store cars and motorcycles as you build up Jason and Lucia’s fleet of personal vehicles. Try to buy some when you can so you can have a wide array of customized bikes, cars, and trucks at your disposal.

You don’t have to, but if you want to do so, just tap left or right to signal to other drivers which way you are turning. In my testing, NPC drivers did seem to react to these signals. One more silly detail in GTA 6.Â

Jason and Lucia can both tag enemies while aiming at them with weapons or using binoculars. This will let you keep track of them and make sneaking around compounds much easier. Oh, and don’t forget to use focus to see enemies making noise and moving around, too.

Binocs can also be used to study the many, many animals in GTA 6 from a safe distance.

When sneaking into a place to rob it, use focus to spot which doors are connected to the alarm system quickly. These doors will glow red. Avoid kicking these doors in and work around them or lockpick them once you have that tool.

Zombix is the in-game medicine that you can pop during combat to heal up. You can find it in the world for free. But if you need some, you can also buy it at stores. Just talk to the clerk to buy some, as it’s often not stocked in the store like food and drinks.

Refueling cars is the main purpose of gas stations, but don’t forget you can also repair your car or motorcycle for a small fee at any gas pump, too. This is often cheaper than using the Scooter Bros app.

In GTA 6, you can hold down on the D-pad to slow down time and see nearby points of interest, missions, and other locations worth checking out. You can also mark any of these spots, and then the game will give you directions via the GPS. It’s faster than opening the map and useful for finding nearby gas stations if you’re running low on fuel.

If you steal a car and you spot a red tracking icon in the bottom left, near the engine and gas icons, you should probably get out quickly. That red icon indicates the car is fitted with an advanced tracker, and police will be able to find you on the map if you drive slowly for too long. You’ll want to avoid these cars until much later in the game when you get the ability to remove these trackers for a high cost. Use the Waink app on your phone by holding up on the D-pad to quickly scan cars and check for trackers.

In GTA 6, cops won’t always pull their guns out and try to arrest or shoot you. Instead, a one-star wanted level can be erased if you just talk to the cop and defuse the situation. Hold the left trigger to focus on the cop (make sure you don’t have a gun out), and you’ll see the option to defuse or provoke the cop. This works on any NPC and might let you avoid violence. Some people will still attack or harass regardless of whether you try to stay calm and defuse the situation, though.

While exploring the map, if you feel a sudden and intense vibration pulsing in your controller, stop and look around with the Waink app. There’s likely some art or something else worth scanning nearby.

Don’t be a litterbug. Giving a hoot boosts your focus and gives you some good behavior points.

While you’ll be able to find similar items and hairstyles at all stores and barber shops, most of these places also have exclusive options available only at that spot. So exploreÂ  and see what you can find.

If you just want a quick and simple trim, you can always look at your mirror in your safehouse bathroom and cut your hair down. You can’t change the style beyond that, though. I guess only the barbers and stylists in Vice City have the magic power to make hair grow back instantly.

Leonida is Rockstar’s digital recreation of Florida. And as someone who grew up in Florida, I was raised to always assume a gator is in every body of water. That’s a good rule of thumb when playing GTA 6, too.

While I encourage everyone to take their time (see next tip), if you really want to get somewhere fast, just use the RydeMe app to call a driver, and then once you’re in the car, hold the left trigger to focus on the driver and get the option to fast travel to your destination for $100.

Listen, how long have you already waited to play this game? Trust me, it’s worth slowing down and taking it all in. There’s so much to see, do, and discover out there, and most of it will pass you by if you speedrun the game.

#3643. World of Warcraft: Forever isn't mere nostalgia bait - it's rebuilding the MMO social architecture that Blizzard spent years dismantling

And when I fall in love, will it be (WoW) Forever?

I don't play video games regularly anymore. Not because I've lost interest in them, but because I no longer make the time, the premium on which has seemed to exponentiate with age. I realised, however, in 2019 that I was a kind of sleeper agent: whenever I heard the opening notes of Legends of Azeroth, the original World of Warcraft login screen music, I would feel the reactivation of a latent part of my mind laid down when I was 10 years old. And so, like a form of possession, whenever Blizzard announces a new legacy iteration of the original WoW, no downpayment in time nor money is too great to prevent me from returning.

Here I am, then, at the launch of World of Warcraft: Forever, seven years after Blizzard first revived the original 2004 game with World of Warcraft Classic in 2019. Once more I set foot on Durotar, to spend as much time as I can levelling up a new Orc Warrior before I am forcibly unplugged by either my boss or, more likely, my wife, and so far it's been a welcome return to some of the frictional - but more involving and consequential - socialising that WoW's decades of updates had previously sanded down.

My relationship with Azeroth began in 2007, when I was ten years old. As soon as I inserted the CD-ROM, I knew that I was going to have to vastly increase my timeshare on the family desktop. For the next six years, school attendance, sleep, and quality family time suffered immensely as I battled to balance my new parallel existence as a member of the Orcish Horde.

It's unremarkable now, but the fact that characters created at WoW's launch are now 22 years old and can still be played in the latest iteration of the game would have been almost inconceivable to many developers at the turn of the century. In the late 1990s and early 2000s, the video game industry was overwhelmingly organised around discrete releases expected to have relatively short lives. For most games, commercial success was concentrated in a brief period surrounding their launch, after which sales declined and eventually ceased. WoW's extraordinary success, and exceedingly long half-life, demonstrated the commercial possibilities and durability of a different model: an evolving, immersive digital environment that players paid to inhabit, year after year. Rather than simply purchasing a finished product, players entered a world that would continue to grow around them. New players, after buying the game (and then its subsequent expansions) and paying for a subscription, could begin their adventures in the same world as those who had been there from the beginning, making their way through its ever-expanding geography and history.

The persistence of Azeroth has been the main driver of its abiding allure for me. I have returned to the game time after time, often just to be enveloped in an audiovisual environment that I know so intimately, and which was so formative in my life. But as the WoW universe was continually developed, the game became increasingly unrecognisable from the version I skipped school to play on Windows XP.

What I wanted from the game had also changed. In a turn that would have been completely anathema to my teenage self, I no longer cared about reaching the endgame or having the most competitive character. I stopped caring about the latest raiding content or PvP rankings. Instead, the elements of the game I had once feverishly tried to skip over, like levelling, professions and story, became, ironically, the only parts of the game that I yearned for.

As time unspooled, WoW naturally needed updates to stay fresh. This meant overhauling many of the unwieldy elements of its original design. Much of this was described as 'streamlining' the player experience, making the game less tedious by reducing downtime and, most critically, reliance on other players.

The original Azeroth emulated the real world in ways that few contemporary games do. Firstly, it was openly unbalanced, with some classes vastly stronger than others, some of which were borderline unplayable. Secondly, it required extraordinary amounts of patience and downtime to navigate. Most importantly, though, it required collaboration with others to get the most out of it. In order to access the latest content, players would have to self-organise into specifically composed groups as big as 40 players large, and schedule lengthy chunks of time each week to make progress.

Over time, much of the original social architecture that forced player collaboration was stripped from the game. Adventurers no longer needed to search for and group up with other players from their own server to complete rewarding content. Automated matchmaking systems increasingly did the work for them.

I remember many late nights when I was prevented from doing something quite modest because there were simply not enough players online, or not enough of the right classes. With my ambitions frustrated, I would often have no choice but to log off and try again in the morning. These frustrations were, I only learnt in retrospect, an important byproduct of inhabiting a world that did not exist solely for my benefit. Other people had their own schedules, priorities and ambitions, and my experience of the game depended on those contingencies.

The changes to WoW followed the trajectory of the wider online gaming industry, where players could increasingly be matched instantly with others at any time of day. These were changes that genuinely respected players' time, but the texture and immersion of the game world paid a hefty price. In making the game more convenient, Blizzard had also made it less necessary, and in some respects less possible, to participate in the social world that had once made Azeroth feel so alive.

It became increasingly clear that there was a subset of players, like me, who weren't interested in seeing an old dog learn new tricks, and just wanted to spend time with the old girl we'd raised from a pup. Even if she did walk slowly, and was a bit blind.

As the years went on, many players moved on with their lives, even if they continued to carry some indelible residue of Azeroth with them. Others created unofficial instances of the original game, known as private servers, and relived those infant years with a knowledge of the world that they could scarcely have imagined possessing when they first entered it. As these servers became increasingly popular, Blizzard, originally very reluctant, eventually launched Classic in 2019, an official revival of the game in something approaching its original 2004 form. Since then, legacy versions of WoW have become popular enough to exist alongside the modern game as a major branch of the franchise.

Re-releasing these legacy versions has been a considerable commercial success. But it also exposed a problem with the project of preservation. The original game, because it is so timeworn, has effectively been 'solved.' Players know almost everything about it, including its most obscure idiosyncrasies, and have found ingenious ways of exploiting them. The uncertainty that once made Azeroth feel so vast and mysterious has been replaced by an extraordinary collective expertise. When new content was added to the game, even the best guilds would spend weeks making no progress. During those early years, players at Azeroth's frontiers had to innovate to find creative ways of tackling novel and seemingly intractable problems.

There are clear limits to simulating a turning back of the clock. Players like me slowly realised that we didn't simply want to return to an earlier, simpler period in Azeroth. We wanted something impossible. Like the characters in Eternal Sunshine of the Spotless Mind, we wanted to forget what we already knew so that we might experience our birth in Azeroth for the first time all over again.

WoW: Forever is an attempt to solve this problem. Like Old School RuneScape, Forever's undeniable forerunner and a considerable success in its own right, it is an expanded re-release of the original game that imagines an alternate future for Azeroth: one in which the game continues to evolve without abandoning the original texture and mechanics, and one that preserves the social architecture that made it so enriching in the first place.

As I write this, my Orc Warrior is sitting at a Campfire, a new mechanic that allows players to establish communal campsites and contribute profession-specific items that confer temporary bonuses to themselves and others. To receive a benefit from Campfires, adventurers are forced to sit together, a deliberate attempt from Blizzard to encourage interactions between players. It is too early to tell how effective this socialising mechanism will be in the long run, but nearly everyone in my experience so far has been eager to shoot the breeze together. I have already shared a number of conversations with other players, most of whom are thirty- or forty-somethings on a similar nostalgia quest as me.

I am playing the game on a laptop using a trackpad, caring very little about efficient or optimal progression. Although I suspect a substantial proportion of the player base shares my approach, not everyone has approached the game so casually. At least five players have already reached maximum level, and many others will have meticulously theory-crafted plans designed to skip straight to the endgame. This is a good thing, and the game should be able to support players with different goals. It's important that the game rewards time and effort, but I hope that the modest amount of time I am able to commit will allow me to feel like I am on my own meaningful adventure, and not a weak player who is trailing behind.

Many in the community have come to believe, perhaps wishfully, that Forever might escape the trap of vertical progression, in which each new wave of content supersedes and renders older content redundant. Instead, the promise of horizontal progression, where new content expands the range of meaningful activities and rewards available without continually raising the ceiling of character power, has been latched on to by members of the community, even though Blizzard's messaging in this regard has not been totally clear.

For players like me, the appeal of horizontal progression is that Azeroth might once again become a place to inhabit, rather than a race to finish. I want to be able to wander off, pursue some obscure profession, or spend an evening doing very little of consequence without feeling that the rest of the world has left me behind. I know I don't have the time to commit to the endgame hamster wheel, and whether Forever will produce a gameworld that meaningfully accommodates players with such different ambitions remains to be seen. But for now, at least, it feels good to be home.

#3642. GTA 6's Japanese version only partially obscures male nudity by putting Jason in a thong, seemingly due to regional censorship

GTA 6 is slowly rolling out across the globe. The crime epic's already available to play in countries such as South Korea and New Zealand, but Japanese players are finding out that male nudity is only partially obscured by a thin black thong that covers Jason and the other men in Leonida.

Last week, we reported that GTA 6 might have been censored in Japan since the region's age rating board lacked any mention of the "sexual content" we knew it would include elsewhere. The Japanese version's install size was also notably smaller than other places in the world.

Now that GTA 6 is finally in the hands of players, we have a better idea of what was left out and/or covered up in Japan. Multiple social media accounts playing the game in Japan have reported that when you take main man Jason into the shower, his butt is only kinda covered up by a thong. At least in the version I played, Jason is usually fully naked while washing up.

GTA 6 censorship on the Japanese version is kinda funny lol https://t.co/u8v0f0cqz0

エロシーンきた！　#GTA6 #GTAVI https://t.co/RKOEtkONlJ

Another social media post spots a different male NPC wearing a very similar black thong during a cutscene that normally has him laid bare in international versions of the game. I'm guessing all instances of male nudity might be obscured similarly in GTA 6's Japanese version.

GTA 6 is far from the only game that's dealt with regional censorship in Japan, however. Baldur's Gate 3 and The Witcher 3 had their most salacious scenes censored in some manner, for example. And even GTA 5 had to remove its infamous torture scene for approval in Japan. It's quite possible GTA 6 has had to cover more than just the backside of nude men to go on sale in the country, although those regional differences won't become entirely clear until players get further through the story.

Ahead of the game's full launch, GTA 6 managed to break Reddit and viewership records on platforms like YouTube and Twitch. Interesting tidbits are also flying out on release day, like the fact you can't replay missions or use cheats until finishing the story. Our Chris Tapsell still had a cracking time with the epic open worlder. "A game of opposites and awe, minute detail and impossible scale, Rockstar pushes back the horizon of video games once again with GTA 6. An irreducible mix of silliness, intimacy, grand ideas and rock 'n' roll action - and a load more after that," he wrote in Eurogamer's GTA 6 review.

#3641. How Am I Supposed To Wait Until The PC Version To Play GTA 6?

I have no desire to be an iconoclast. Today’s launch of Grand Theft Auto VI is by far the biggest release in all of gaming history, and on pre-orders alone it’s already the biggest game of 2026. It’s the most expensive game ever made, and it seems inevitable that it’ll be the highest-grossing game ever released. Not only that, but it’s also extraordinarily good. It’s a pinnacle in gaming, and it’s going to be the focus of the worlds I exist in for months to come. Of course I want to be a part of this. But I also want to playÂ GTA 6 for the first time on PC.

I’ve always playedÂ GTA games on PC. Partly because I sometimes didn’t own the relevant PlayStation at the time, and partly because the first 20 years of my career were primarily spent covering PC games. But also because the PC versions were always better. That’s not some silly factional position, or dumb anti-console nonsense, but rather just a statement of fact. Rockstar would put out the console version, then spend six months removing all the artificial limitations and adding all the features that had remained stuck on wish lists, and then let the game loose into the unfettered technology of personal computing. The PC release is always the definitive version of any Grand Theft Auto, complete with six months of bug fixes on top of the myriad improvements, and what better way to first experience a great game than in its finest form?

Except, is that even realistic this time? Let’s entirely put aside the notion that as some manner of “games journalist,” it’s arguably important that I be culturally aware of the biggest game release ever. I’m also a person who wants to enjoy a game in the way he wants to enjoy it. But dear god, the pressure to play the moment my clock hits midnight. Heck, for me that’s five hours earlier than it is for folks in the U.S.! I’ll be ahead of the curve! And everyone else I know will be playing this game in every moment they can. The mimetic pressure alone is overwhelming.

This time I certainly do own the console, and although my PS5 doesn’t get a lot of use (here again I appear to have accidentally gone against the curve, but I just find my Xbox Series S and Game Pass to be a much more attractive prospect), it’s there and ready to offer me a game that a few of my colleagues have already finished and assure me I’m going to adore. And I want to be adoring it! Zack’s review is making this all the harder for me, as he so beautifully describes the minutiae of the game, the smallest details that seem so deeply attractive. I’m so astonished to learn that each of the two main characters has their own distinct social life, and can get up to their own business while you’re playing as the other. I want to experience that! And I can, in just 12 hours’ time. But…I want to experience it at its best, and I can’t for at least five more months.

I’m so torn! There’s absolutely no part of me that thinks it’s somehowÂ interesting to not play GTA 6. Ooh, look at me, the artisan gamer in his beret as he plays an obscure Welsh-language art-house experimental game that muses on the notion of grief and ontology, and not yourÂ mainstream gaming. No, not that at all. I just want the first time I play the incredible game to be as incredible as possible, and I know that the PC version will be a big step up, even from the incredible application of six-year-old tech on display in the PS5 version. The PC version will be designed to use day-old tech, pushed to work with the most recent graphics card and RAM you’ve been able to cobble together, and heck, it might even run at over 30 FPS.

But I’m not even driven by the tech. I just…like playing games on PC. It’s the machine I played games on as a teenager, and the machine that gave me a career writing forÂ PC Gamer and foundingÂ Rock Paper Shotgun. I love my PC. I like playing games at my desk, on my ultra-wide monitor, whether I’m using mouse/keyboard or a console controller. I get curling up on the couch and enjoying games that way, but there’s something about the intimacy of the screen being two feet from my face, not the other side of the room, that draws me further in. There are fewer distractions in my teeny office, carved into messy shape over years of gaming and working. And that’s another thing! It’s a far safer way to play a game like GTA 6 when there’s a 12-year-old in my house who cannot comprehend why I might not want him watching, let alone playing. A 12-year-old who wants to be camped in the same room as my PS5, playingÂ Minecraft on his Switch while on the phone to the other kids in the same realm. That’s no place for some 18+ gaming entertainment.

So what should I do? I still don’t know. My instinct is that I’m going to give in, fork out the Â£70 ($92) for a copy, and then be really annoyed with myself whenever the PC version does come out. I’ll have only been able to play the PS5 version in fits and starts, given the availability of the living-room TV and the appropriateness of who else is in the room, or I may sacrifice any notion of sleep and play the game nocturnally, frustratedly squinting to read the inevitably tiny text on the more distant television, knowing that it just won’t be the same to play it over again. But if I don’t, obviously everything that’s still a surprise will have long been spoiled for me by the time I play, and I’ll be missing out on the excited conversations of friends and colleagues who will be sharing amazing moments and crucial discoveries.

Bigger than that, I’ll not be part of the cultural zeitgeist, this enormous moment of shared entertainment that will beÂ everywhere, referenced inÂ everything, and by all accounts, utterly, stunningly good. And that sucks. But [wrinkled nose, sulky tone] I want to play to play it on PC. I just wanna. It’s not fair. I’m completely stuck about what to do.

Steal your first aircraft close to your GTA 6 starting point.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

If you've just started GTA 6 you might be wondering where the nearest airplane and helicopter are located to your starting point. There's a huge new world to explore, and the best way to do it is by air. But first, you've got to find a plane or chopper to steal.

Luckily, there's a reliable spot to snag your first few aircraft close to your starting safehouse, and you can probably steal them without raising a single alarm.

You'll drive about 2.5 miles southwest from Jason's house in Key Lento. Start the trip by driving southwest through Key Lento, then west through Abismo Key, and finally west and then north to Southwind.

You'll be taking Sunbelt Highway (Route 1) the whole way and you'll know you're close after you cross two long bridges. Southwind is a small district located next to the Mile Zero Air Station: GTA 6's military base.

(Yes, the military base has planes and helicopters too, but it's a little trickier getting your hands on them so check out our GTA 6 military base guide before you attempt it.)

The highway will make a bend to the north as you enter Southwind. On your right you'll see a concrete barrier alongside the road, and where it ends is where you want to turn right into the parking lot, at the sign for SBW (Sherwin Boatworks) and Chicki's Tiki Bar.

If you're facing the water (east), on your right (to the south) is a small hangar with (typically) a few Mammoth Dodo seaplanes parked inside and around it, and often a couple more moored off the dock. Seaplanes aren't the fastest planes in the game, but they're perfect for early exploration because they can land on both water and land, and they require almost no room to get airborne.

Keep up to date with the most important stories and the best deals, as picked by the PC Gamer team.

There's never anyone hanging around here, either, so you won't draw any attention if you help yourself to one of these planes. Just drive one into the water and take off, or steal one from the dock.

Follow the same instructions to Southwind as above, but instead of looking to the south, look straight east from the entrance to the parking lot. There's an open gate leading out to a dock where a Buckingham Maverick helicopter is sitting.

Just ignore the no trespassing sign, run over to the dock, and hop into it. Now the skies are yours.

Chris started playing PC games in the 1980s, started writing about them in the early 2000s, and (finally) started getting paid to write about them in the late 2000s. Following a few years as a regular freelancer, PC Gamer hired him in 2014, probably so he'd stop emailing them asking for more work. Chris has a love-hate relationship with survival games and an unhealthy fascination with the inner lives of NPCs. He's also a fan of offbeat simulation games, mods, and ignoring storylines in RPGs so he can make up his own.

The announcement that Hoult and Holly recently welcomed twins was not made by the couple themselves but by comedian Pete Davidson. Sitting alongside Hoult at a junket for their movie How to Rob a Bank, Davidson offhandedly mentioned that his costar was now a father of four. (Hoult and Holly previously welcomed two children, born in 2018 and 2022, respectively. They have kept details about all of their children private.) "[Nicholas is] a great dad, father of four,” Davidson told Entertainment Tonight, adding, “[Nicholas has] four under what? 7 [years old] … which is nuts.” Davidson also offered some hints about the timeline of Hoult and Holly becoming parents again, revealing they'd already welcomed their twins before the former SNL star and ex-girlfriend Elsie Hewitt's daughter, Scottie Rose Hewitt Davidson, arrived last December. “Elsie was pregnant while we were filming and [Hoult] just had his twins,” Davidson recalled. “He would fly back every weekend to go see his family, and that was very inspiring and awesome.” Hoult nodded along to Davidson's unintentional announcement about the birth of his and Holly's babies but offered no further context. Us has reached out to Hoult's representative for comment.

The Challenge alum Nicole Zanatta welcomed twin daughters Seraphina and Madyson on May 1.  “Becoming their mom has been the greatest blessing of my life, but our journey hasn’t been easy,” Zanatta wrote via Instagram on June 1. “Both of my girls were diagnosed with congenital CMV (Cytomegalovirus), a virus I had never heard of until it became part of our story.” She continued, “Since birth, we’ve spent time in the NICU, attended countless appointments which are still ongoing, undergone testing and started medications. I recently brought them home a week ago, but our journey is far from over. Through every high and low, I choose faith over fear, resilience over doubt, and gratitude for every blessing along the way. I will give my girls every opportunity to thrive. I will always fight for them and advocate for their needs.” According to the Mayo Clinic, CMV is "a condition caused by a common virus.” The CMV virus stays in the body for life once a person is infected and can spread through body fluids, including blood, saliva, urine, semen and breast milk.

#3638. Zara Tindall Shows Cheltenham Why She's The Queen of Race Day Dressing

Zara Tindall didn’t let the cold snap stop her from enjoying a day at the races on Friday. Accompanied by her close friend Dolly Maude and country-set favorite fashion designer Jade Holland Cooper, the daughter of Princess Anne and granddaughter of Queen Elizabeth II brought a dash of regal glamour to the proceedings following a glitzy night out in support of Prince William.

And while the sun may have been out, the Olympic equestrian still needed to wrap up against the chill. Tindall opted for a long plaid coat from L'Agence, a Purdey roll-neck jumper in brown, and a fascinator from Sally-Ann Provan. She accessorized with a new pair of Hector Lion earrings, a new Fairfax & Favor handbag, and completed the look with leather boots, also from Fairfax & Favor.

Zara Tindall joined in the action at Cheltenham Racecourse on Friday

Dolly, on the other hand, wore an avant-garde feather coat with knee-high boots and what looked to be a pair of emerald tights.

The pair were last spotted together in October, when they attended the William Hill Showcase Meeting at Cheltenham, but their friendship goes way back. Long considered Zara’s best friend, Dolly became Princess Anne’s lady-in-waiting in 2024. A former NHS midwife, she helped to deliver Zara’s third child, Lucas Tindall, on the floor of Zara’s bathroom at Gatcombe Park after the plan for the birth went awry in 2021.

Jade Holland Cooper and Zara Tindall on day one of The November Meeting at Cheltenham racecourse

But Dolly’s bond with the niece of King Charles III goes back long before that. (Not for nothing did Zara’s husband, Mike Tindall, joke that the 53-year-old is “more important than I am.”) Dolly was Zara’s maid of honor when the pair tied the knot, and when Zara split from her then-fiancé, jockey Richard Johnson, in 2003, the pair moved in together—they still live close by in the Cotswolds.

Having worked as a maternity practitioner in the NHS in Gloucestershire for 13 years, Dolly also did some philanthropic work using her maternity expertise, working in the unit of a hospital in Kambia, Sierra Leone for a month in 2013. At Kambia, she taught staff basic nursing skills. Before qualifying as a nurse, Dolly studied fashion and Cordon Bleu cookery at Eastbourne College of Food and Fashion, graduating in 1989.

Zara Tindall also braved the stormy weather for a day at Cheltenham with Dolly in October

Dolly Maude is known for her love of horses—a passion she shares with Zara and Princess Anne—and is often seen in Ascot’s royal box alongside the Princess Royal. In March 2024, she made her first official appearance as the Princess Royal’s lady-in-waiting, a momentous occasion that marked a new phase of her enduring bond with the royal family.

The royal confidant has four children with her husband Chris: Billy, who studied at Swansea University; Nell, who trained at the Central School of Ballet; a keen skier, Ted; and Mary.

Princess Anne's daughter wrapped up in a warm plaid coat and roll-neck jumper

Concerning Dolly’s appointment, another friend of Mrs. Maude's told The Telegraph, “She’s such a great girl. For the Princess Royal, it’s a perfect fit because of their shared love of dogs and horses. She’s not only extremely close to Zara, she also gets on brilliantly with the Princess. She’s fiercely loyal and discreet. It’s a great match.”

While much of Zara Tindall’s time this season has been spent touring the country’s most prestigious racing meets, she still found time to support her cousin, Prince William, at one of his treasured annual traditions. The Prince of Wales helped to put together the Tusk Conservation Awards at Raffles on Wednesday night and invited Zara to the celebration of conservation, alongside Lady Amelia and Lady Eliza Spencer and the Marchioness of Bath.

Dolly Maud made her debut as lady-in-waiting for the Princess Royal at the 2024 Commonwealth Day Service in March

Zara showcased her characteristically elegant style, donning a sapphire-blue Rebecca Vallance short-sleeved midi number, aptly named the “Crown Jewel” dress, which she paired with Kiki McDonough earrings. It is not the first time that the royal has lent her support to Prince William’s second-longest patronage: she also joined the crowd at the Tusk Awards in 2025, donning Rebecca Vallance again, and tearing up at the Prince of Wales’ speech in honor of those who gave their lives as rangers.

Zara Tindall and the Marchioness of Bath at the Tusk Awards

Maura Higgins became a quick fan favorite on Dancing with the Stars, but I'm worried she could miss the Season 35 finals. With the semifinals and one vote before the finale, I'm afraid her run on the 2026 TV schedule may be at an end. Now, it seems I may have more reason to be concerned about what lies ahead.

On the heels of a tough Grammy night featuring the "Thong Song," it was clear Higgins' rib injury was more than a storyline for DWTS to play up. Now, per a new rumor from The Sun, Higgins allegedly had to cancel a rehearsal and seek medical attention while preparing for Dancing with the Stars' semifinals. Her rib was reportedly re-injured over the weekend, leaving some questions about how she'll be able to perform during the live episode.

As viewers learned in last week's episode, Higgins didn't break her rib, but the swelling and damage caused so much pain that she briefly considered throwing in the towel. It'd be a shame to see, given just how far she's come since the beginning, but obviously, her health takes priority.

As of late, I've written about how Tatyana Ali and Jan Ravnik's advancement could set up a fan favorite going home instead of them on Semifinals night. Maura Higgins and Mark Ballas were on my shortlist of people who could go home, and honestly, I think it's all going to come down to who gives the best performance.

I Thought I Knew Who I Wanted To Win DWTS Season 35. But One Comment Totally Changed My Opinion

One can never rule out the impact of fans, however, and I do wonder how this rumor could impact their thoughts on whether she should advance. Part of me thinks she could gain sympathy, assuming she wants to keep going, and get the pass to have another week to recover, give it her all, and try to win DWTS on finale night.

Conversely, I could see some viewers deciding it's her time if the performance is weak or if it's evident that she's struggling with an injury. I would see sending her home as more of an act of mercy at that point, rather than putting the pressure on her to drop out of the finale.

All this to say, I'll have all eyes on Maura Higgins as the DWTS semifinals play out. There's so much chatter happening online about who could go home, and this situation is just another layer to consider. I even think there's a possibility that Harry Shum Jr. could miss the finale, which makes the prospect of this episode so much wilder.

Dancing With The Stars airs on ABC and Disney+ on Tuesdays at 8:00 p.m. ET. This is going to be the biggest episode of the season thus far, so make sure to clear that primetime schedule to see what happens!

Magic: The Gathering's Universes Beyond line goes beyond the final frontier.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

I recruited the biggest Star Trek fan I know to help me road test the new Magic: The Gathering set. Right away he was impressed by cards that referenced the Star Trek: Prodigy cartoon and Star Trek Beyond—a third movie in the J. J. Abrams-verse I completely forgot was even made—but if that kind of trainspotting was all it took to make a successful crossover then people would have liked the Spider-Man cards a lot more than they did.

What makes the better Universes Beyond crossovers work is how they bring out the themes of their source material, turning motifs into mechanics that make a set feel like a genuine expression of the thing being adapted rather than just another property being fed into the content machine. Having played some games with the cards, yeah, I think Star Trek works.

I built a blue-green deck around Strange New Worlds, a mechanic that rewards you for having different lands rather than just stacking Islands and Forests. When I played Deep Space Scan I drew a card for each differently named land I had, and those lands also lowered the cost of powering up my Astute Terraformer.

Meanwhile, the Federation mechanic gives bonuses for having different creature types on the table like Vulcan and Klingon and Romulan (though not Borg). With just those two mechanics, the set emphasizes exploration and diversity. You really do want to put together a crew representing multiple species and send them into the final frontier. (There is of course a card called Final Frontier.)

Star Trek also makes use of the spacecraft mechanics introduced in Edge of Eternities, where a ship starts with limited capabilities but has to be stationed by tapping creatures to add charge counters to access its full abilities—like flying and fighting. Lt. Cmdr. Geordi La Forge is a solid combo, doubling the amount of charge counters you add each time and letting you get the Enterprise into the air twice as fast.

There are cards for various different iterations of the Enterprise, but I'm partial to U.S.S. Enterprise-A, Free Spirit, because when you play it you get three red 1/1 officer tokens for free. That makes it faster to station, and after that you've got three disposable officers to chump block with. Which is why they're red.

There's also a Beam Me Up mechanic to bring a card back from the discard pile at the cost of returning a card from the table to your hand, and a cute assimilate mechanic that lets you wipe creatures' existing types then turn them into artifacts under your control for your Borg deck. But what makes the Star Trek cards feel like Star Trek is how much they emphasize teamwork.

Keep up to date with the most important stories and the best deals, as picked by the PC Gamer team.

The Common Goal card lets two creatures deal damage together, and there's a whole suite of cards that get better when you've got creatures with a total power of 8 attacking as one. Worf, Honor-Bound Warrior, who doubles his own power when he's part of that attack, proved a gamewinner for my red/white deck more than once. The thing that really comes across is Star Trek's utopian ideal of everyone pulling together in a crisis and being better for our differences. It's optimistic, with stars in its eyes, and even a casual Star Trek watcher like me can appreciate that.

Magic: The Gathering's Star Trek set is available now, for both tabletop Magic and Arena.

Panettiere's celebration of life happened in late September.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

Back in August, the public was devastated to learn that actress Hayden Panettiere died at age 36. This was a huge shock, especially considering her brother died just a few years earlier. Fans are still mourning and re-watching her work on projects like Heroes, and plenty of people were surprised when Panettiere's mother Lesley Vogel didn't attend her celebration of life back in September. Now Vogel is speaking out and explaining her absence for the services.

Fans still have questions about Hayden Panettiere's death, and were curious about why her mother wasn't in attendance for the late actress' funeral services. Lesley Vogel recently appeared on Inside Edition, where she explained why she chose to opt out of her daughter's celebration of life. She was quoted saying:

I just didn’t want to rock the boat either; it was probably for the best.

During the interview, she shared that she and Hayden Panettiere drifted away from each other after the Scream actress' relationship with ex Brian Hickerson started picking up. They mother and daughter seemingly had a difficult relationship, some of which was mentioned in the actress' memoir This Is Me: A Reckoning. Still, it was surprising for some that Vogel didn't attend the funeral services.

While appearing in the same interview, Lesley Vogel claimed that she was indeed invited, but didn't think her presence would be helpful during this difficult time. She went on to say:

I knew that some of the people there wanted to believe I was the horrible mother because Hayden was angry and made statements.

Clearly this was a complicated situation, which might explain why Hayden Panettiere's mother ultimately decided not to attend her funeral. She knew there'd be discourse about her either way, but is seemingly at peace with her decision. Inside Edition contacted Brian Hickerson for a comment, but did not hear back from him.

Panettiere's death hit the public hard, largely because she grew up right in front of our eyes, including early roles in projects like Remember the Titans and A Bug's Life. Millennial fans in particular grew up alongside her, and there was a ton of love her work on Ice Princess, Heroes, Nashville, and the Scream movies (the latter of which are streaming with a Paramount+ subscription). Folks were thrilled when she reprised her role as Kirby Reed in Scream VI, with Panettiere thanking fans who "came to her rescue". Clearly she's someone who meant a great deal to her fans, many of whom are still processing her death. As for Lesley Vogel, she's given an explanation for missing her late daughter's funeral.

Hayden Panettiere's legacy lives on through her various acting credits. Heroes is streaming on Netflix, while Nashville is over on Pluto TV. Our thoughts continue to be with her loved ones as they mourn and grapple with the loss.

#3633. As Hollywood Battles AI, Pedro Pascal Says Making Behemoth! Filled Him with “a Tremendous Amount of Hope”

Pedro Pascal says that the character he plays in Behemoth!, his first leading film role, is the “closest thing to me that I’ve ever done.” And because of this, “the experience on set felt surreal in a sort of physically tangible way,” Pascal told the audience during a Q&A at Vanity Fair’s Screening Room at LACMA on Saturday.

Directed by Tony Gilroy, Behemoth! tells the story of Alex, a prodigal cellist who returns to Los Angeles and the world of Hollywood film scoring after decades performing symphonic work around the country.

“The mixing of my own life and this person's life, I've lived a very nomadic one. Don't ask me where home is. And so that felt like it was crossing personal lines for me in a way,” he continued during a post-screening discussion about the film, which featured Pascal and writer-director Tony Gilroy, moderated by VF's West Coast Editor John Ross.

But according to Gilroy, their collaboration on the film almost didn't happen, thanks to an alleged missed connection at a Star Wars event.

Tony Gilroy and Pedro Pascal  at Vanity Fair's Screening Room at LACMA on November 14, 2026

“We went to a Star Wars convention in Tokyo where we took Andor,” recalled Gilroy. “There was this big Disney dinner so all the Star Wars people are there and [Pascal] was kind of busy and flighty.”

“I had the flu! I flew from London to Tokyo!” Pascal countered.

Gilroy continued: “He seemed like he was so hip that he didn't come to the dinner. I thought, 'Oh he's got such a great thing going on he's going to some better party; he's not going to a boring dinner.'”

As the audience laughed, Pascal was quick to set the record straight: “I cannot believe that you thought that I ditched that dinner. I was doing re-shoots of Fantastic Four!” he said. “They flew me to Tokyo that night and flew me back and I was on a set. [Turns toward the audience] Can you believe this?”

“Oh my God. I'm calling Kathy Kennedy [the President of Lucasfilm] right away,” Gilroy joked.

Luckily, the moviemaking stars (and schedules) aligned and the pair was able to make their personal, moving film with Pascal serving as Gilroy's “exclamation point. He has all the sadness and all the covering that this character needs to have and the nomadic life.”

Pedro Pascal, Tony Gilroy and John Ross at Vanity Fair's Screening Room at LACMA on November 14, 2026

Pascal and Gilroy formed a genuine bond and are very comfortable making playful jabs at each other, keeping things light but also expressing their gratitude for being able to make Behemoth! their way, in Los Angeles, where the film and television industry has been struggling to regain a foothold. Despite the challenges, past and present, they are holding out hope for human-made storytelling to foster further human connection.

“People's natural resistance to the robot takeover is clear,” said Gilroy when asked about the rise of AI. “I don't know what's going to happen. I really don't. The music scene out here is the coral reef of what's happened. It's been dying out here for the last 15 years… It's grooving a little bit now. I think people want humans. I don't know what's going to come back, but this is this incredibly humanizing element of movies that's happened. Can it be replaced by AI? Probably, quite shockingly, simply. There's probably an emotional amplitude knob on some f—ing algorithm, but this movie is organic.”

Pedro Pascal and Tony Gilroy  at Vanity Fair's Screening Room at LACMA on November 14, 2026

Pascal walked away from Behemoth! feeling optimistic. “The experience of shooting this movie definitely injected me with a tremendous amount of hope,” he said. “We weren't making money on this movie. Nobody was. And you had the most expensive people involved in this film because of their talent and their experience. So there was just this purity of love in the work from every single department, and that was incredibly contagious. And it was primarily locations, and so Los Angeles was just constantly revealing itself in all of these magical ways because we were so location-based. I had shot a series in Colombia for three seasons, and I would argue that the primary character of that series, Narcos, was shooting it in the country of Colombia because there was only one way of capturing that energy and that physical story. And LA did that as well. And then it's so tender. I think the story is incredibly tender. Would you ever expect it from this guy [gestures to Gilroy]?”

“Oh my God. What a cold, weird thing to say,” the director joked.

“There are other movies this year that I think in their own way, movies that I've seen this year that I love so much, that fight for humanity and the storytelling,” Pascal continued. “So I think that there is a sort of pushback that could be really, really thrilling as far as [creativity] is concerned, as far as politics is concerned. We want to be human beings and we want to be connected to one another and we want to tell each other's stories and witness each other's stories and we want to look after each other and all that shit. That's my hope.”

Tony Gilroy at Vanity Fair's Screening Room at LACMA on November 14, 2026

Gilroy had another suggestion: “Blow up the AI centers, man," he joked. “I don't mean to blow them up. I mean blow them up at the voting box. Go and vote and blow them up. Go see the Musk documentary, man. Go see that, watch the whole four hours. I'm pitching my movie [here], but watch that movie.”

The inaugural edition of Vanity Fair’s Screening Room pairs this year’s most compelling films with a slate of programming that includes post-screening panels and conversations with actors and filmmakers. The invitation-only events are welcoming an audience from the worlds of film, fashion, culture, politics, media, and tech, much like the magazine itself.

Following the program in Los Angeles, Vanity Fair’s Screening Room will arrive in New York, where screenings and events will take place at Cherry Lane Theatre from December 4–6.

The last time we got a decent look at Total War: Warhammer 40,000 was the Gamescom build, which Fraser Brown called the highlight of his year. Since then Creative Assembly has continued iterating and a more recent build was subject to a friends-and-family playtest, then shown off in an "alpha strike" livestream that lasted a solid hour and 20 minutes.

Beginning 23 turns into an Ultramarines campaign, we got to see the battle for the Praevoss system, which has three conquerable planets in it—as well as a gas giant and a dead world that can't be fought over.

Each system in Total War: Warhammer 40,000 gets a separate narrative, a mini-campaign that plays out before you move on to the next system, taking some but not all of what you've built with you. That seems like an interesting way of dealing with the grand strategy problem of campaigns getting boring when you've painted half the map, but still have 100 turns before the end. Having a soft reset and facing different foes in a different theatre would keep a campaign feeling fresh.

In the Praevoss system the Ultramarines' objective is to liberate Imperial planets from an ork scourge. When the marines take a region, one of the options they have is to "scour the battlefield" in return for a big payout in Requisition, at the cost of raised Suspicion. Calling down a fleet bombardment to soften up orks ahead of the battle also raises Suspicion because there are still civilians in the area. Oops.

It's an interesting part of the fiction to emulate: Imperial planets having their own governments and maybe resenting the transhuman giants who've been sent to liberate them. Space marines have gone rogue before—the head of the Astral Claws chapter infamously hoarded planetary tithes for himself and became known as the Tyrant of Badab, and of course there's the whole Horus Heresy thing—and a random Imperial governor might not be thrilled at the angels of death stomping across their world.

Playing nice prevents Suspicion from going up and rewards the marines with Influence points, which they spend to gain reinforcements from local Imperial troopers. That seems super useful because of another way Total War: Warhammer 40,000 emulates the fiction, which is making space marines difficult to replace.

Where other factions replenish losses after battles, the marines are much more limited. It takes a decade to train each one after all, and there are only so many progenoid glands to go around. The livestream shows that while some casualties return after battle thanks to their transhuman physiology letting them survive injuries that would normally be fatal—and as we've already seen, important characters who fall can be jammed into dreadnoughts—actual reinforcements have to be called down from the orbiting fleet. They can even arrive mid-battle via drop pods that slam down right on top of the enemy.

Keep up to date with the most important stories and the best deals, as picked by the PC Gamer team.

The Total War: Warhammer trilogy is all about making each faction play differently, and I'm glad to see that carry over even to the vanilla Ultramarines. The customization options, which let you outfit them with bespoke wargear loadouts, speak to a similar dedication to detail.

What's missing from the livestream is any suggestion of fleet battles in Total War: Warhammer 40,000. The ships in orbit seem to play an important part in the campaign, but as a source of reinforcements and bombardments and a way of moving armies between planets. I guess if we want to play 40K ship battles Battlefleet Gothic: Armada 2 already exists and is quite good.
