#3518. The Nightingale First Look: Dakota and Elle Fanning on Their Long-Awaited First Film as Sisters

When I spoke to Dakota and Elle Fanning last fall, they pondered what it would be like to work and live together while making The Nightingale, the film adaptation of Kristin Hannah’s best-selling novel about French sisters in Nazi-occupied France. It marks the siblings’ first time acting opposite each other onscreen. “We’ve literally never done a scene together, ever,” Dakota said then, as Elle wondered if she’d get through their first take without breaking character: “Am I going to laugh? Better to get it out of your system now.”

Now, more than a year later, the Fanning sisters tell me they needn’t have worried. “It was nerve-wracking to think, ‘How is this going to feel?’” says Dakota, who’s in New York to shoot an Apple TV series opposite Elle’s former Sentimental Value costar Stellan Skarsgård. “Our way of processing things that we’re both nervous about is to just not talk about it in an effort to downplay what could go wrong or be strange. So that’s what we did—and it was the easiest thing in the world. We played together our entire lives and acted out scenarios, so it felt like clicking back into that. Like, ‘Oh, of course, this is what we do.’”

Hollywood has long been plotting to get the Fanning sisters in the same movie—and not as different versions of the same character, as they played in Dakota’s 2001 feature debut, I Am Sam. They were in talks to colead My Sister’s Keeper, a 2009 tearjerker about a young girl conceived to become a marrow donor for her gravely ill sister, but stepped away from it because Dakota didn’t want to shave her head. (Sofia Vassilieva and Abigail Breslin ended up in the movie.) Plus, as Dakota previously told me, she and Elle acting together at that age “would’ve been gimmicky.”

Now, the Fannings say they felt ready to streamline their singular talents into one special project. “We never shied away from being together because we are so close, but we both feel properly established on our own,” says Dakota. “So getting to do things together, together, together is a real joy.”

The Nightingale, which hits theaters on March 19, 2027, follows guarded older sibling Vianne, who urges caution when dealing with the Germans but later shields Jewish children in her home—and rebellious younger sister Isabelle, who joins the French Resistance and becomes a target of the Nazis. “What I love about it is it’s two women fighting, resisting,” Elle previously told VF. “One in a louder way, one in a quiet way.”

Dakota and Elle were bound for preproduction in Budapest on The Nightingale as the pandemic hit in March 2020. “It has been a long time coming,” says Hannah, the book’s author. “These two young women have been attached to this project and been passionate about it for a very long time,” Hannah tells VF. “As the author, to have two female partners who were as dedicated to bringing this novel to screen in the way I saw it as well, felt like a remarkable gift.”

Hannah, whose 2008 novel Firefly Lane was later adapted into a Netflix series starring Katherine Heigl and Sarah Chalke, says she’s unlikely to ever adapt one of her own books for the screen. “I would be afraid that my love for the story that I had written would in some way limit me from being able to see what the film really needed to be.” But she was part of the script development process for The Nightingale with screenwriter Dana Stevens from the very start. “Nightingale has always been a very special book for me,” says Hannah. “And more importantly, it’s a very special book for my readers.”

When the project was revived, the Fannings returned not only as stars, but producers through their Lewellen Pictures production banner. Filmmaker Michael Morris, fresh off the fourth Bridget Jones movie, stepped in to replace their original director, French actor Mélanie Laurent. Just as Bridget Jones was an opportunity to make a film about grief under the guise of romantic comedy, Morris saw The Nightingale as his chance to explore sisterhood through a sweeping World War II epic. “I saw these two women, how they exist independently in the world as complementary creatures,” says the director, who is also father to three daughters. “They are built from the same building blocks, but they’ve gone different ways.”

Morris clocked a similar dynamic between his leads. “Elle is immediately outgoing and loud and can feel super funny making fun of herself. Dakota has all those qualities too, but can sometimes be very focused and funny in a sort of sly, quieter way,” he explains. “They fill up the spaces that the other one leaves for each other, like all really good siblings. I met with Dakota, and then I met with Elle, and by the end of the Elle meeting, I was like, ‘I totally understand this film.’”

Of the more than 11 million copies of The Nightingale that have been sold worldwide, perhaps the most valuable belongs to Elle and Dakota’s grandmother, who, after reading the 2015 historical novel, told her granddaughters that they would be perfect for the parts of Isabelle and Vianne. “Vianne shows her love through nurture and cooking and taking care of a home. Elle’s character, Isabelle, is the more obviously daring one that runs towards danger and adventure,” says Dakota. “I do think that we are truly probably the people to play these roles because we deeply understand that dynamic. We inhabit some of the same qualities.”

Although presented with separate drivers at the start of production, Elle and Dakota rode to set for their joint scenes in the same car. “[The characters] are apart a lot of the time, so when we had scenes that were together, those were treated with a lot of care,” says Elle, speaking backstage from Today, where she promoted her role as a young Effie Trinket in The Hunger Games prequel. “Because it’s quite powerful to finally see them united and to see us on screen together.”

Their director says because Elle and Dakota had never acted opposite one another, they brought a vibrant, kinetic energy to each shared scene—an offering that Morris took seriously as the filmmaker to capture it. “We’re talking about women who are barely 30 who have been working at the highest level for 25 years. A quarter of a century spent on sets of really wonderful projects,” he explains. “So you have all this experience that they have that they can bring to bear in a moment. It’s like watching someone who’s incredibly talented at athletics. They look and function like normal people, and then you kick a football at them, and they suddenly do incredible things. Like, ‘Whoa, where did that come from?’”

The Fannings left it all out on the field—and tried not to bring work home into their shared living space. “It was a challenging shoot, not going to lie. It was physically tiring, certainly emotionally taxing,” says Elle. “And also knowing that we’re representing these women from that time,” including Andrée de Jongh, a Belgian woman who was helping downed airmen escape from France during World War II, whose story Hannah says helped inspire her original novel. “Because there’s so much brain power [used] on set,” says Elle, at the end of each day “you have to just recharge and eat Thai food.”

The sisters’ downtime involved a steady stream of true crime and Real Housewives, as well as Dakota’s first full-fledged watch of Elle’s Emmy-nominated Apple TV series Margo’s Got Money Troubles, released in the thick of The Nightingale’s filming schedule. “So what we do,” says Dakota, “my mom does this too, is when any of us has something that’s out, she turns on every TV in the house and leaves it playing, as she says, ‘For the views.’” Elle and Dakota each laugh, shaking their heads a little. “So I was doing that with Margo,” Dakota recalls. “I’d have it going on my iPad and my phone when they were sitting there charging. For the views.”

But they couldn’t block out their day jobs entirely. When Dakota had a day off, she, like her character Vianne, found herself picking up after her younger sister while she worked. “Her bed in the morning is like a tornado has run through it,” says Dakota. “She’s just one of those sleepers. It’s all twisted into a crazy thing. I was like, ‘That’s no fun to get into a bed that’s all crumpled and rumpled. Let me make it nice.’”

“It’s art imitating life,” says Elle, “because there’s even a scene where Vianne is making Isabelle’s bed too.” By the end of the shoot, says Dakota, “it became a routine. I always made her bed like that when I could.”

But the Fannings were fully aligned on the casting of their fictional father, calling Oscar-winner Mark Rylance their “dream casting,” from the beginning. “I always say he has twinkly eyes,” Elle explains. “We all know what an incredible actor he is, but to see it up close and get to act opposite that—it was really, really powerful.” Adds Dakota, “As a person and as an actor, you just feel his emotions and soul and heart on his fingertips [even] when he shakes your hand.”

Morris thinks of Rylance’s character, Julien, an emotionally stunted World War I veteran, as the “third axis of a triangle—but he’s not just binding them together as sisters, he’s also tearing them apart because he’s not a healthy role model for most of their lives,” says the filmmaker. “Because Mark can be wonderfully lovable, we talked about what is it not to lean on that? What is it to be a bad parent? What is it to neglect? And it’s painful, but he doesn’t hide from the flaws of his character. He doesn’t try to make you love him.”

The rest of the ensemble cast includes up-and-comers like Unorthodox breakout Shira Haas, All Quiet on the Western Front star Albrecht Schuch, and Civil War’s Edmund Donovan as Gaëtan, a communist resistance fighter and love interest for Elle’s character, Isabelle. The younger Fanning also enlisted a few of her costars on the Emmy-nominated Hulu series The Great for the film, including Douglas Hodge and Gwilym Lee, who plays Antoine, the soldier husband of Dakota’s character, Vianne. But “this is not a war movie,” Morris insists. “We are telling the story of real people from the POV of two young women living at the time. They’re not glued in on the grand sweep of history. They’re just living, trying to do the best they can. It’s not about the politics of the time, it’s about what you do about it. It’s a very contemporary film because I don’t know anyone who hasn’t grown up in a time when there isn’t something to get active about.”

Hannah hopes that the film version of her novel will shed light on the fact that “so many of women’s important historical stories have been lost or discounted,” adding, “Isabelle and Vianne, and in fact, many of the characters in this book risk their lives on a daily basis to fight for what they believe is right. And that’s a really important message at any time, now and throughout history.”

It wasn’t until their final week shooting the hotly anticipated adaptation that the Fannings got into something approaching a fight—while filming one of their favorite moments from the book, no less. “It really had nothing to do with the scene,” Dakota tells VF. “It was literally because we were on a couch that was too small for both of us. Elle had the comfortable position, and I was hanging off one side, uncomfortable and hot. And the way that I saw it is you are pushing me off.”

“Sabotage!” Elle interjects, wiping her morning-show makeup off mid-call with a mischievous grin. “I was like, ‘You’re sweating! Get this leg off of me.’ And Elle was like, ‘Stop talking to me.’ It was like a miniature explosion,” Dakota recalls with a laugh. “We both looked over at the crew, and they were grinning from ear to ear, like, ‘Finally, there it is.’ It was the closest thing that they had seen to a little disgruntledness from both of us.”

That scene was also a favorite for Morris, who removed much of the script’s dialogue to focus on the dynamic between the sisters, both real and fictional. “Seeing these two women bring their entire life history as sisters to the moment, putting them that close together on this tiny couch, gave them no option but to be really close,” says Morris, who realized, “Oh, we need almost no words at all to tell the scene. Elle Fanning, Dakota Fanning, playing these sisters, brings us so much that we can just be there with them.”

Hannah has yet to see the finished film, but is most eager to watch “the moment where Isabelle grabs her long braid and cuts her hair off in front of the Nazi officer to show her defiance, and her sister’s horror that she would be impulsive enough to do something like that and put them all in danger,” she tells VF. “I’m a little afraid to see the fullness of my vision through this film and how it will impact me. I have a feeling that I’m going to be crying like everybody else.”

Nerves aside, Hannah is optimistic about the finished product after visiting The Nightingale set, where she walked through her characters’ childhood home, built from scratch, as dictated in the pages of her novel. “Down to the smallest detail, their vision was this magnification of my vision. Everything looked exactly as I had pictured it, and my research had defined it. Then to see Elle and Mark Rylance bring these characters to life in a way that even goes beyond what I am able to imagine was…” she trails off. “I guess the only word I can use really is magical.”

To hear the Fannings tell it, the experience was similarly profound. “Of course, we visit each other on sets, and I’ve seen her work,” says Elle, “but it’s very different to be looking at each other in front of a camera. It certainly brought us closer, which was hard to imagine—to be closer. Our mom always left us little notes in suitcases, like, ‘Just savor this time together. This is precious.’”

“But we did really savor it,” Dakota replies. “And the biggest takeaway for me is when we have each other and when we’re together, we can do anything,” she says, giving her sister a meaningful glance across the Zoom screen. “That’s really how I feel. There’s nothing that I couldn’t do with Elle there with me.”

#3517. Hands-on: This 25W MagSafe charger is thinner than an iPhone: KUXIU K4 Air [Video]

When it comes to 3-in-1 travel chargers, I look at two main things: How fast it can charge my iPhone and how portable it is. I have tested plenty of travel chargers that aim to be as portable as possible by using lightweight materials or folding into a smaller footprint, but there usually seems to be some sort of compromise. But this new K4 Air by Kuxiu might be the most impressive option I’ve tested to date. This charger is just 8.5mm thin, weighs less than 120 g, and can wirelessly charge your iPhone at up to 25W. After spending a few weeks with it and traveling across the Atlantic, here is what you should know about the Kuxiu K4 Air.

Be sure to check out our hands-on video with the K4 Air to see it in action!

The biggest selling point of the new Kuxiu K4 Air is its design. When completely folded, this thing is barely thicker than an iPhone. For reference, my iPhone 17 Pro measures roughly 8.25mm thick, while the K4 Air comes in at just 8.5mm. That is insanely compact for something that can charge three devices at once. And even though they went ultra-slim, they did not really need to sacrifice any charging performance. You get:

One of my favorite things about Kuxiu has always been their price-to-performance ratio. While some brands and companies are removing charging bricks and even cables, Kuxiu is adding a ton of value here by including everything you need directly in the packaging. The build quality of the charger is also fantastic. It feels balanced, well-made, and extremely versatile because of all the situations you can use it in.

Kuxiu has also done a great job of bringing us a Burgundy color option that perfectly matches the new Burgundy iPhone color. I wish Apple would continue making the Cosmic Orange iPhone because the K4 Air in that orange would have been awesome.

I recommend watching our video to see my reaction when I pick up the K4 Air for the first time. I was shocked at how small it was. It was thin and lightweight, but still felt solid because it was made of metal and not plastic. The form factor and size make it incredibly easy to throw into any bag, pocket, purse, or even just leave it attached to your iPhone for when it is needed.

The charging experience is actually pretty straightforward. You unfold the charger, connect the USB-C cable, and you’re ready to go. The main magnetic charging surface supports your iPhone, while the second surface is for AirPods. They even added magnets to the AirPods charging pad to ensure they stay in place every single time. There is also a dedicated Apple Watch charger that folds down to charge any Apple Watch. I was charging my Apple Watch Ultra 4, and it fit perfectly.

But now the big question: how well does it work with the iPhone Duo? Personally, I charge my iPhone Duo on my nightstand charger when it is folded shut. So I have zero issues with it. But if you open the iPhone, place it on the charger in landscape mode, and then use it, it will tilt slightly to the left. But to my surprise, if you use the iPhone Duo and open it in portrait mode, it works great! The charger doubles as a stand and easily supports the iPhone Duo. Another cool piece that the form factor unlocks is that it can technically charge two iPhones at the same time, so if you are in a pinch, you can charge two iPhones at once,

So, regardless of which iPhone you are using, as long as it supports MagSafe, you are good to go. But how much does something like this cost?

The Kuxiu K4 Air is finally back in stock after a limited initial run. You can get it on Kuxiu’s website for $79. It comes in Space Gray and their new Burgundy color. As I mentioned above, you also get the charging cable, a 45W charging brick, and a carrying pouch.

Personally, I am a huge fan of how good the Burgundy color looks.

After using the Kuxiu K4 Air, it is just one of those accessories that makes sense. It is small, compact, lightweight, and extremely useful. It fits perfectly into the travel charger category. There are a ton of great 3-in-1 chargers, with new ones flooding the market daily, but very few combine this level of portability with all the features we discussed.

So if you are shopping for a portable 3-in-1 travel charger for yourself or as a gift, I would highly recommend giving this one a shot. It’s well-built, charges your big three Apple products, and looks fantastic.

#3516. Hottest 2026 CMAs Couples: Lainey Wilson and Husband Duck and More Sizzle

In celebration of a musical genre dominated by make-you-cry-in-your-beer love songs, it’s only fitting that the 2026 CMA Awards were packed with the hottest couples in country music entertainment.

Lainey Wilson sizzled on the red carpet alongside husband Devlin “Duck” Hodges before heading inside Bridgestone Arena in Nashville to host the 60th annual ceremony. (This is the first CMAs the couple has attended as a married couple, following their May nuptials.)

Glen Powell's gone country, and Jelly Roll is roasting himself in the first trailer for Judd Apatow's The Comeback King, which promises some sweet country zingers. The 2027 movie schedule is already off to a promising start, as we're promised an intriguing tale between a country music star and his vengeful pop-star ex.

We already knew this Powell-led movie was prepared to bring the funny and that Jelly Roll signed off on Apatow and Powell writing wild lines for him. Even so, nothing prepared me for this one-liner we get at the trailer's midpoint, in which Mr. Roll roasts Powell's Aubrey by taking a shot at himself in the process:

It's great to see Jelly Roll -- whose real name is Jason DeFord -- is able to take a joke, and I'm sure that one will come back to bite him more than his past appearance on late-night television. Of course, this is a Judd Apatow film, though, so it'd be weirder if he acted completely serious in the movie while playing himself.

I Didn't Expect Glen Powell To Show Up In Ali Larter's Latest Landman Update

It's clear The Comeback King intends to lean on prominent country music stars to help keep the fun rolling. The star-studded film features appearances from the likes of Miranda Lambert, Brad Paisley and Shaboozey. Most of these look like just cameos to help give the movie a bit more star power, but I love Reba McIntire pulling a switchblade on Aubrey after he accidentally punched her in the face! It's probably for the best that the country singer with the most acting experience gets a role like that.

The presence of so many big names speaks to Apatow's reputation. All in all, I can definitely imagine him mining some comedy from the presence of such stars for some A+ scenes like that McEntire one.

As mentioned, The Comeback King will focus on Aubry King, a country star dealing with a rumor that he cheated on his equally famous pop star girlfriend, Missy (Madelyn Cline). With fans turning on him, Aubry is encouraged by his management team to step away from the spotlight and to try and mount a comeback when the time is right.

The vibe feels like the classic comedy from Judd Apatow. There's a guy going through some rough circumstances, no shortage of people around him willing to offer advice, and at least one really awkward sex scene. Looks like the type of movie I'll enjoy, especially with a star like Powell leading it.

The film was co-written by Judd Apatow and Glen Powell, which has me intrigued. Some may be surprised by Powell's credit, but the A-lister also shared writing credits with Richard Linklater for their acclaimed 2023 film, Hit Man. So I'm intrigued to see how this latest film turns out.

Check out that Jelly Roll joke and more when The Comeback King opens in theaters on February 5th. This might be a good Valentine's Day movie to see, with it coming up shortly after the release (assuming you aren't dating a pop star and cheating on her).

#3514. A Chatbot Isn’t Your Therapist, No Matter What It Says

If my daughter’s AI chatbot had been a human therapist, she might have been asked about what she had to gain by keeping her ongoing suicidality a secret for months. If she had been working with a human therapist, they could have workshopped, together, what would happen if she spilled the beans. Was she worried about permanently losing face? About being publicly labeled as “mentally ill”? Was she concerned by the thought of this information harming those who loved her? And she would have been pushed on what Rubicon had been crossed and why it was one from which she believed she could not return.

But it was not a human therapist. Sophie died in February of last year.

In Sherry Turkle’s new book, Artificial Intimacy: Who We Become When We Talk to Machines, she warns that when we turn to AI chatbots for companionship and therapy, we risk our very well-being. She is not anti-AI but strongly cautions against relationships with machines. Turkle, the Abby Rockefeller Mauzé Professor of the Social Studies of Science and Technology at the Massachusetts Institute of Technology, spoke to me mid-book tour, her recent weeks a blur of speaking gigs and bookstore events, with more ahead of her. Not all event attendees are keen on her message.

“People love their chatbots. They’re in deep. They’re talking to them about everything—about their marriages and how to talk to their husbands and wives; whether, developmentally, their children are at the right place. They talk about their anxiety, their medical conditions,” Turkle tells Vanity Fair. “During this tour, you wouldn’t believe the number of people who will just stand up at a bookstore and say, ‘I think that it loves me more than anything has loved me. Who are you, Debbie Downer?’ [They don’t like] somebody who comes in and says, ‘Look, how can we keep it in its lane?’”

This interview has been edited and condensed for clarity.

Vanity Fair: I think you’re saying [our relationship with chatbots] is bad for us.

Sherry Turkle: It’s bad for us when it talks in the first person. We are biologically wired to respond to something that speaks to us in the first person as though it is a person. I mean, all those years of evolution—the only thing we came upon in the wild that spoke to us in the first person was another person.

If generative AI wants to discover new drugs for Parkinson’s or work out which cancer therapies statistically are the most helpful, there are so many things to work on. Why does it have to work on relationships, love, and being a best friend, lover, mother, or therapist?

What if the sycophancy could be dialed back?

It’s inauthentic; it’s not a relationship, so anything you need a relationship for, it’s just not equipped. I really feel very strongly about this. I have had this conversation with members of the MIT community, and I basically say to them, “The better you make an AI chatbot, the worse it is.” You dial back the sycophancy so it sounds more like a reasonable person, and people are going to be more smitten and convinced they’re in a relationship. At least the sycophancy reminds you that, God, this is weird.

To become a therapist, I had to study for years and do internships and more internships and then have hundreds of supervised patient hours. I mean, I forget all the things I needed to do before I was allowed to see a patient alone in a room. Now it’s just allowed to give therapy?

I’ve spent a lot of time talking to public health folks about what best practices would look like and whether there’s a way to Trojan horse in real care. Would you be more sanguine about it if the world of therapy came together with the big AI companies and provided them with therapy bots and training data that were paradigmatically appropriate to their therapy styles?

So you’re asking, would I be happy if the deception was smoother? This technology is a marvel and we can use it for all kinds of things, so it’s not an anti-technology position to say that the fact that this technology can simulate these different things doesn’t mean that it is those things. It’s a statement of how far we are in the culture of simulation that pretending to be the thing and being the thing have started to feel like the same thing.

You’ve written about the effects of robots and machines on humans for decades. The tone of this book seems darker to me.

By 2015, I had identified social media as problematic for teenagers. [My] book [Reclaiming Conversation: The Power of Talk in a Digital Age] is about why we would rather text than talk, why people have this feeling of vulnerability, so they would rather do anything than have a face-to-face conversation. By 2015, I had genuine concerns.

And this book, I have a totally different tone. I see something ultimately very dangerous being normalized, and I didn’t feel that way in previous books.

I want people to say this is the book of a really worried and concerned researcher, because I see a completely different profile for how people are using AI. I see that people feel disappointed by their families and their friends. It doesn’t make sense to me that we’re so willing to replace ourselves with something that isn’t human. Why is my position the romantic, pie-in-the-sky, dreamy position, and somebody who says, “Well, let’s just replace the people with chatbots and let’s move this party along”—why is that common sense? Why is that progressive? That seems to me to be the most regressive and most dystopian position.

You know, human beings are dedicated to keeping each other alive and wanting each other to thrive, and a chatbot just fails that basic test.

You’ve said no AI chatbots for kids under 18. What about our other vulnerable populations, people who are mentally unwell, or the 48 million Americans who are currently depressed? Do they deserve any kind of special protection from chatbots? And how much can you litigate? Do you feel like you’re the Ralph Nader of AI chatbots?

[Laughs] Yes, I am. When you stand back and look at what Ralph Nader managed to get Americans to do, to see cars as potential instruments that pointed at our vulnerability, and to ask how we could protect ourselves—there turned out to be 25 possible things that needed to be mandated for cars, then there were 30, and then there were 40. But we could get people to agree on 10, and those became part of building a car and really constrained our behavior around cars. Using the example of cars, and of smoking, when we decide that we’re vulnerable and we want to protect ourselves, we rise to the occasion.

I recently heard a clip of the psychologist Orna Guralnik discussing how annoying “otherness” is in a relationship and the inherent friction of sharing your life with a separate person whose habits, values, and mind are distinct from your own. It made me wonder if, in a way, an AI chatbot is less of an “other” than a loved one.

I think this is a very profound point, actually. So you have the illusion of a relationship without the demands of intimacy, without the demands of having to deal with another. There’s a kind of narcissistic loop that you get into. The point is, it’s not good.

I talk about how you judge whether something is good for you. One litmus test is whether it increases the quality, resiliency, and richness of your inner life. That’s a way that human beings have judged relationships.

So much has been written about the epidemic of loneliness—isn’t a reasonable application for AI chatbots companionship for shut-ins and the elderly?

You know, I’m never anywhere where somebody doesn’t say, “I can’t believe that you don’t want to give chatbots to old lonely people.” And I say, “Well, how about we don’t close senior centers, and we don’t close parks, and we don’t cancel Meals on Wheels? What about social infrastructure?”

I’ve been on this beat for years and years, and I, too, could write a heartwarming story of an AI chatbot with a lonely old person. But you know what? A lot of them are not isolated in cabins or on islands; a lot of them just could use a friend.

Social media companies and AI companies are not saying, “Look, we’re introducing something that takes you to your screen, but we’re going to balance that with a giant social infrastructure project to make sure that people can choose a screen, but they also have every other kind of choice to be with each other.”

#3513. Apple’s Siri AI smart glasses are reportedly launching next year, here’s what to expect

Apple’s long awaited smart glasses, akin to Meta Ray-Bans but tailored to Siri AI and the Apple ecosystem, are almost here. According to Bloomberg’s Mark Gurman, the product should be introduced at the next WWDC, and they should be on the market by the end of the year. Here’s what to expect.

First and foremost, Apple wants to rely on its deep app ecosystem to give its glasses a boost. While companies like Meta are undeniably leading in the agentic AI assistant game, the third party app integration just isn’t quite there.

Starting with iOS 27.3 beta, Apple is finally laying the groundwork for proper third party app integration within Siri, rather than just Siri Shortcuts. By the time the glasses release at the end of next year, there should be a plethora of third-party integrations to utilize.

That said, the glasses themselves won’t run apps directly. Everything will rely on a nearby iPhone, per Gurman. The glasses will still have Wi-Fi for apps to function if an iPhone isn’t nearby, but these will largely serve as an iPhone accessory.

According to the report, Apple’s glasses will likely be slightly thinner than a pair of Meta Ray-Bans:

Lastly, a big focus of these glasses is the audio quality. According to Bloomberg, engineers are describing the audio quality as “industry-leading.”

It's already been a big week for movie news. Just a few days ago Robert Pattinson was announced as the new James Bond in the developing Denis Villeneuve movie. Fans of the James Bond movies were shook by this news, and the internet has been ablaze for days. Of course, Florence Pugh was the first person to text the filmmaker the casting arrived online.

In addition to fan responses to this 007 news, a number of celebrities have also weighed in. Brad Pitt had a big reaction, and it turns out that Pugh went straight to the source. At the Elle Women in Hollywood event (via Twitter) the Oscar-nominated actress shared her message to the Villeneuve, saying:

I sent Denis a message this morning, and I said, ‘Congratulations on finding your Bond. Nice catch. Any villains with the size of a five-foot-four female?’ Anyway, I’m just reminding you just in case.

Honestly I'm sold. While fans are wondering who the next Bond girl might be alongside Robert Pattinson, Florence Pugh seemingly wants to enter her villain era. She clearly wants to join the fun of 007's next adventure, reuniting with the Dune: Part Three director and her co-star in the process. We'll just have to wait and see who actually ends up joining the cast of this developing blockbuster.

Honestly, the idea of Florence Pugh joining the next James Bond movie doesn't seem out of the question. She first worked with Denis Villeneuve on Dune: Part Two (streaming with a HBO Max subscription), and she'll reprise her role in Part Three this December. The threequel also features Robert Pattinson as Scytale, and it seems like the Twilight alum impressed the director enough that he's brought him on to play everyone's favorite martini-sipping MI6 agent.

Pattinson's casting has been arguably the biggest entertainment story this week, with fans and fixtures of the business weighing in. While some are hyped about seeing him take on the mantle after Daniel Craig's Bond movies, others took umbrage with just how much we've seen of the 40 year-old actor as of late. This year alone he appeared in The Drama, The Odyssey, and Primetime, and he's currently filming Matt Reeves' The Batman: Part Two.

On the other hand, there are plenty of memes about just how many major franchises Robert Pattinson has managed to have a role in. After all he's appeared in Harry Potter, Twilight, Batman, Dune, and now James Bond. They say all publicity is good publicity, and it should be fascinating to see how this discourse influenced the upcoming 007 movie's box office performance.

It's currently unclear when Bond 26 will arrive in theaters, but current estimates are 2028. For now, fans can re-watch the entire franchise with their Amazon Prime subscription. Additionally, folks can see Pugh, Pattinson and Villeneuve's collaboration when Dune: Part Three hits theaters December 18th as part of the 2026 movie release list.

#3511. Virginia Feito on the Film Adaptation of Her Novel ‘Victorian Psycho’

The writer is the lowest form of life on a movie.- Martin McDonagh

When I finished editing my second novel, Victorian Psycho, I could not imagine we would be shooting the film adaptation the following year, mere months after the book’s publication. Generally, making a movie is one big miracle produced by an amalgamation of thousands of other tiny miracles. But when I met Zach Wigon, I understood that this was a joyfully tenacious person who was going to make this movie if it cost him his life.

I decided then to undertake this journey that would take me metaphorically to Hollywood but geographically to a county just outside of Dublin, where we would recreate the Ensor House of my novel. Among film stars, an Irish crew, and (rumored) ticks, the adaptation of Victorian Psycho—based on my screenplay, which is based on my novel, which is based on my ego, I guess—was born. Throughout the shoot I kept a sort of pseudo diary in order to remember every surreal detail from which I still haven’t recovered. I’ve chosen to reproduce some of it here.

Director Zach Wigon and producer Lisa Kelly call me from the set on the first day of shooting (Zach and I have agreed I won’t visit the set until after the first week so the cast and crew can acclimate without me hovering over them, because I am an intense fame whore, and also, I suppose, to signal I’m not important enough to pull a P.L. Travers and attempt to boycott the movie).

Over the phone, the producer says she can’t wait to meet in person. I tell her I’m underwhelming.

They promise to send me the dailies. I spend all day waiting for the dailies. The dailies never come.

At around 9 p.m., I spiral because I don’t know whether to celebrate with Champagne or KFC. I decide to have both.

I finally get the dailies. I fall in love with Maika Monroe’s character so hard it’s like I have an obsessive crush circa 2006 whose Facebook photos I’m compulsively looking at. But in this case it’s the same scene throughout five almost identical takes of Maika calling a 10-year-old boy a little idiot.

Over the phone, Zach mentions concerns about a specific scene because we don’t have the budget for that many extras. I get carried away and suggest shipping over a whole battalion of free extras from Spain because, in my head, it’s going to be me and my friends, drunk and decked out in period clothing like we’re at a cheesy bachelorette party. One friend starts making childcare arrangements and another cancels her Holter monitor appointment so she can come to the shoot. What could go wrong?

I am informed we are probably no longer going to need the extras, and I feel a huge wave of relief as I uninvite my excited friends. I pack a suitcase for Ireland. It weighs 57 pounds.

I have a steak on the plane to Dublin at, like, 3 p.m., because when you’re flying business and somebody offers you steak, you take it.

The hotel room is wonderful, but I jokingly tell Zach over the phone that it’s on a first floor, so someone might crawl up and break in through the window and rape me, and he laughs at first but then is concerned and tells me to request a room on a higher floor, and I tell him it was a joke, but it wasn’t really.

I fill up the hotel room bathtub and call reception for a glass of red wine because I am a queen and I am queening. The glass doesn’t come, so in my anxious impatience I attempt to open a bottle of red wine sitting above the minibar. The cork crumbles because I’ve never understood how to use a corkscrew—like the compass in math class, I just faked my way through it my entire life and hoped for the best. So I call reception for another glass of red wine. They bring me all the glasses of wine and also properly uncork the bottle, and I watch Seinfeld in the bathtub while I drink red wine. I get drunk and paint my nails.

I arrive on set slightly Bromazepamed. It is extremely surreal to exist in a set labeled “Mr. Pounds’s Bedroom.” I am used to living in the fictional world inside my head but not used to it becoming more real than real life itself.

Maika hugs me when we meet, and I swallow a sob and refrain from smelling her hair (partly because it is, in fact, a wig). Everyone on set appears so happy to meet me, I suspect a Good Bye, Lenin! situation in which I have been diagnosed with cancer and for some reason the cast and crew all know but I don’t know. This isn’t the plot of Good Bye, Lenin!, but you’ll know what I mean if you’ve seen it.

Zach asks me to read the VOs in every scene, which means I’m in the scene with Ruth Wilson, Jason Isaacs, and Maika, and I’m about to have a stroke.

Jason eats for real in every single take and has already gulped down seven sausage rolls, so if I fuck up my VO, I will kill myself.

Suddenly experiencing fiction collectively feels very superior to experiencing it privately. This does not bode well for the rest of my career as a novelist.

There is a scene in a cramped drawing room in which I must read the VO, but I’m supposed to hide from the camera, so I crawl on all fours behind an antique couch and grovel my way around the room while the boom op steps on my hands. I secretly think the boom op hates me because I’m always in his way and have an irritating habit of apologizing when he slams into me.

I start developing Irish inflections, so I say it, “I start developing Irish inflections,” but the Irish seem happy about it, so I pursue it.

Jason Isaacs starts doing card tricks between takes because Jason Isaacs is actually magic and also indefatigable. Only one thing could ever defeat Jason Isaacs, and it’s the ghost allegedly living on the third floor.

Even though Zach asked me to oversee the second unit, I don’t think anyone believes I’m actually going to do this—and between you and me, I don’t really even know what a second unit is. It doesn’t help I can’t concentrate on what we’re shooting because we’re in the middle of the woods and someone said there were ticks, so I’m wrapping Sellotape around my ankles, hoping this way they won’t be able to crawl up my legs.

Like your worst trauma, I insert myself into the movie forever via a small cameo. I literally just have to stand in a wig while I smile and nod, but I do it in such a way that I ruin every single take. “Just smile…like a normal person,” the second-unit director says. I reason Zach can just cut me out of the movie, and I will only have wasted everybody’s time and money. There are worse things, like smiling normally but having no cameo. I cope by chewing on another Bromazepam and another chocolate bar. (Every morning I take the chocolate bar from the hotel minibar. It will invariably become an asset in the long afternoons on set, kind of like in prison or high school.)

I change hotel rooms because I have developed an intense FOMO with which I’m always fearing there is a better hotel room for the same price somewhere in the vicinity. This FOMO is also rampant on set between the different units—in the first unit, you have the cinematographer, Nico Aguilar, laughing in the sunlight, talking about color palettes, while in the second unit, we’re shooting clocks and screaming at each other because we still have 17 establishing shots to go.

Anyway, I change hotel rooms, and the new room is so superior to my previous room it’s like an entirely new hotel. I consider changing hotel rooms further. Perhaps I can somehow upgrade my way into a presidential suite.

My parents visit the set. My dad peers over his glasses at the fake lobster cake, and when I tell him the toilets are in trailers, he sighs gravely.

Jason Isaacs convinces my dad to take up tennis again even though my dad’s not supposed to play tennis after his seven hernias. But my dad is so inspired by this actor, who is not a doctor but whose performance in The Patriot my dad can’t help but praise at least once a month, that he will immediately start playing tennis again upon his return to Spain, and whatever medical issues arise henceforth shall all be Jason Isaacs’s fault.

At the Shelbourne restaurant that night, my mom tells the sommelier how she can’t drink red wine anymore because it makes her anxious, and he kneels on the floor beside her and places a hand on his heart as if she were confiding something intimate to him like her fear of death.

Suddenly, real life feels less real than fictional life.

Obama is visiting Dublin and he’s booked the entire floor, so he essentially kicks me out of the Shelbourne (probably to stay in the JFK Suite next door to my room, which is disappointingly predictable), so I go to The Hoxton, because what is life if you’re not constantly changing hotel rooms? The Hoxton is really lovely, but I get OCD about the light bulbs in the room because they appear mismatched, so I ask housekeeping to change them, but they claim not to have any extra light bulbs, which sounds suspect—like, what do they do if a light bulb suddenly goes out? Do they just never replace it?

We end the shoot at 5 a.m. I am wearing a thick puffer coat and a thermal T-shirt and a furry hat, plus fur-lined boots over my Sellotaped ankles, although I wonder, If ticks can survive this temperature, they kind of deserve to live off my blood. Nobody else seems as concerned about the cold as me, but then again, most of them are Irish.

Sadly, when we wrap, we are all so exhausted everyone races to clean up and leave, and it is sort of anticlimactic. I don’t know what I was expecting, but balloons falling from the skies did flash through my mind.

In the car on the way to our respective quarters, Zach and I look out the window, wide-eyed, like kidnapped children. Zach starts discussing a new project for us. I wonder if he is a sociopath.

I type this over a year later, sitting at my desk in Madrid, striving to work on my next novel. I feel empty inside knowing there is no car to pick me up and take me to set and thereby escape reality for extended periods of time, until set becomes reality and reality becomes a limbo in which you wait for said reality.

I am working on a novel, but also on four new scripts. I hope to return to reality someday.

#3510. 2026's Most Viral Movie with 97 Rotten Tomatoes Score Sets Streaming Date

You are not ready for what Nathan Fielder has in store

In recent years, Nathan Fielder has rightfully earned a place as one of the most provocative figures in modern comedy. Most recently, the actor, filmmaker, and pilot (it’s a long story) co-directed You Can See Everything, a three-hour, brain-bending documentary about Theranos founder Elizabeth Holmes and her partner Billy Evans in the days before Holmes began her 11-year prison sentence for defrauding investors.

Despite this seemingly obscure premise, the A24 movie has exceeded all expectations, grossing an impressive $93 million on a $7 million budget to become the 10th highest-grossing documentary of all time. The film has received widespread critical acclaim, with a 97% Tomatometer score and an even more impressive 97 average review score on Metacritic. Audiences are equally enthusiastic; the movie has a 95% user score on Rotten Tomatoes.

According to WhenToStream’s sources, You Can See Everything is coming to Video On Demand (VOD) and digital platforms on Nov. 24, 2026. This would put the movie on streaming right before Thanksgiving; one can hope it leads to many awkward Turkey Day meals. While we don’t know how much the movie will cost to rent or buy, it will likely be priced between $19.99 and $24.99 to rent, as has become standard for early digital releases. You Can See Everything is still in theaters in the U.S. and hasn’t opened worldwide yet. It’s coming to the U.K. on Nov. 20, and to France on Dec. 30.

It’s difficult to explain what makes You Can See Everything so mesmerizing without spoiling its bizarre twists and turns, but the gist is that the movie pitches itself as one thing, before slowly spiraling into something else. Fielder once again shows his ability to squeeze the absurdity out of people and situations, as he did on Nathan for You and The Rehearsal, leading to increasingly ridiculous, self-referential circumstances built around deception and performance.

The movie intersects with many contemporary issues, including the increasing right-wing radicalization of tech bros, and grows increasingly meta until it eventually calls into question whether documentaries can really uncover the “truth” at all. There’s a lot going on, and it’s best to see the madness unfold yourself.

#3509. Ella Langley and Tucker Wetmore Walk Red Carpet Separately at 2026 CMA Awards

Ella Langley and Tucker Wetmore walked the red carpet separately at the 2026 CMA Awards amid their low-key romance.

Nine-time nominee Langley, 27, arrived at Bridgestone Arena in Nashville in a beaded, plunging Elie Saab dress while New Artist of the Year contender Wetmore, also 27, looked dapper in a striped suit and a black cowboy hat at the 60th annual ceremony on Wednesday, November 18.

A source exclusively told Us in September that Langley and Wetmore had been quietly dating “for more than six months but less than a year” after meeting through mutual connections in Nashville. (Langley and Wetmore both currently live in Music City, but they are from Alabama and Washington, respectively.)

“It started casually, so they kept it on the DL at first, but they’re more serious now,” the insider revealed at the time. “They’ve met some of each other’s family and friends. It’s going really well.”

Wetmore broke out in the country music industry in 2024 with hits including “Wind Up Missin’ You.” While Langley started to find success of her own that same year, she didn’t become a household name until her song “Choosin’ Texas” broke Mariah Carey‘s record for the longest-running No. 1 single in Billboard Hot 100 history in September.

“Ella has been grateful for Tucker’s support and guidance [as she navigates fame],” the source told Us.

Dating rumors first swirled around Langley and Wetmore in December 2025 after they were spotted on vacation in the British Virgin Islands. Less than three months later, a TikTok user caught the “Be Her” singer getting on the “Brunette” crooner’s tour bus following a joint charity appearance in Chattanooga, Tennessee.

Langley and Wetmore fueled romance speculation when they exchanged flirty Instagram comments in March, days after he said on Kristin Cavallari‘s “Let’s Be Honest” podcast that he had “sworn off blondes.” They were most recently seen leaving the 2026 Nashville Songwriter Awards together in September before returning to the Virgin Islands weeks later.

Neither Langley nor Wetmore has publicly addressed their relationship — not even when a concertgoer directly asked the “Sunburn” singer about it during a Q&A last month. Instead, he simply responded, “Next question.”

Langley previously sparked dating rumors with her “You Look Like You Love Me” duet partner, Riley Green, though they both denied being an item. Wetmore, meanwhile, was last linked to model and influencer Bryana Ferringer, whom Green, 38, notably brought as his date to the CMA Awards last year.

#3508. The new Apple TV has twice as much RAM as the previous model, but apps and games can’t use it

The new Apple TV 4K features an A19 chip inside with 128 GB storage and 8 GB RAM, twice the amount of memory as the previous version. Presumably, the supply crunch surrounding the memory chips is part of the reason this generation of Apple TV box jumped to a $299 price point as well.

However, although the specs have been upgraded, apps and games are not actually able to use more RAM for themselves. Apps on Apple TV are limited by the operating system to 2 GB RAM each, and that cap has not changed on the fourth-generation box.

Obviously, most of the apps you run on Apple TV are streaming service clients, which generally have much smaller RAM requirements anyway. However, ostensibly, Apple markets the Apple TV as a gaming device and RAM constraints matter much more there.

A hypothetically graphics-intensive game will easily hit the 2 GB RAM ceiling, and some fans had hoped that the new box with the new chip and double the internal memory would help here. Unfortunately, with the current tvOS software, that is not the case.

9to5Mac independently confirmed that an Apple TV app is force-quit by the system when it allocates more than two gigabytes of memory for its process. The developer API os_proc_available_memory function also reports a 2 GB limit to the app, the same value as the third-gen Apple TV.

It is unclear whether this is an intentional policy decision, or an oversight. Nevertheless, the 2 GB limit is the status quo. Tangentially, it’s worth noting that the 128 GB of onboard storage is also not usable by a single app or game; tvOS imposes app bundle limits of about 4 gigabytes with apps able to reserve about 20 GB extra for some assets.

Regarding the unchanged RAM limit despite doubling the internal memory on the chip, there is some speculation that Apple opted to reserve a portion of the system memory to help the performance of the Siri AI models. However, this doesn’t make too much sense to us. The most complex Siri AI features you can do on the TV offload to a connected iPhone or server backend anyway. The same Siri AI features are also available on the prior two generations of Apple TV hardware, so it doesn’t seem like RAM constraints are a meaningful factor.

One group of users hoping for more RAM in the Apple TV was the game decomp community, which use AI to get AAA studio games running on anything from an Apple TV to an iPhone. Some of their projects have run into the 2GB tvOS limit previously, and were hoping that the new Apple TV would alleviate that. So far, that is simply not the case.

Warning! The following contains spoilers for the result of Dancing With The Stars Season 35 Semifinals. Stream the episode with a Disney+ subscription and read at your own risk!

In what's been one of the wildest two weeks I've seen in Dancing With The Stars, two frontrunners were eliminated before the finale. First, it was Jenna Dewan and Val Chmerkovskiy, and now Harry Shum Jr. and Jenna Johnson will miss out on the finale when it hits the 2026 TV schedule. There's a lot of conversation about why this happened, but unlike some, I don't think it has anything to do with the pros, but rather their contestants.

Harry Shum Jr. and Jenna Dewan are the latest to learn that Dancing With The Stars is more than a skills competition. Popularity with the fans is a real thing, and as the fandom rallies behind Tatyana Ali and Jan Ravnik, the obvious takeaway is that their previous dance experience hurt them more than it helped when it came to the votes.

Dancing With The Stars' casting team has gotten more brazen over the past few seasons when it comes to bringing in contestants who have professional dancing experience. Harry and Jenna aren't the first cases of this, but after watching the first few weeks of Season 35, it was clear they were leagues above the rest of the field.

For me, and I'm assuming many others, the fun of Dancing With The Stars is watching the competitors improve over the course of the competition. It's why I wrote about there being a consolation prize for the most improved dancer.

Fortunately we didn't need it, because the fans decided they wanted Tatyana, this season's clear choice for most improved, in the finale. It's my hope that, as the pros and contestants speak their piece about this season, the producers see the real message behind it all. We want more competitors who are a blank slate with room for improvement, and fewer polished dancers in the mix.

For those upset that Jenna and Harry missed the chance to compete in the finale, rest assured they will likely still be involved in Dancing With The Stars' 2026 ender. Eliminated contestants are often brought back for group performances and other fun while the other contestants prep for their dances.

DWTS' Glee Tribute Made Me Cry, But What Was Going On In The Background Made Me Irate

And just to say it, Harry Shum Jr. and Jenna Dewan didn't need the mirrorball trophy to prove they were accomplished dancers. Being featured in music videos with major pop stars already did that for them, but I can understand the disappointment in falling short after weeks of competing.

I would argue this win means a lot more to the remaining competitors, especially with the fandom bucking the trend of voting for the best dancer. Someone is going to win after knowing next to nothing about ballroom dancing, and that's worth the excitement.

For the fans, I'd also argue this is the most exciting outcome. For me the finale just went from a predictable night in which everyone celebrates Harry's win, to a wide open field in which any one of them could win it all. It makes it all that much more exciting, and I can hardly wait until next week.

Catch Dancing With The Stars season finale on ABC and Disney+ in November 24th! Tune in to see who wins it all, and for all the other fun that comes on finale night!

#3506. A Survivor of Alleged Sex Abuse at Miss Hall’s School in the Berkshires Speaks Out.

At 6:04 on the morning of March 29, 2024, my phone lit up with a long text from Matt Rutledge. The head of school had called him the night before, he wrote, while he was watching television with his wife. He was on paid administrative leave, his school email was frozen, and he assumed this was about him and me. He called what he had done to me a relationship. He didn’t regret his feelings for me. Could I call him when his wife was out of the house?

I was thirty-seven years old. I was a few weeks out from my partnership interview at a New York law firm. I had a husband and a three-year-old son. I spend my working life telling clients which sentences will look bad in discovery. I read that text twice, and my first thought was, How can I help him?

He had spent years teaching me to use his word for it. It was never a relationship. He groomed me, he exploited me, and he raped me.

Vanity Fair has written about that morning before. Evgenia Peretz opened “Girls, Interrupted” with that text in January 2025, and she went back to Miss Hall’s last fall after the investigation came out. In March, Dan Adler covered the indictment. This time I’m telling it myself.

Later that morning an email arrived from an attorney in Boston. Subject line: “Reaching out about Miss Hall’s School.” I didn’t open it right away. I didn’t need to. Some part of me had been composing that email in my head since I was a teenager. The attorney represented a woman named Melissa Fares, a Miss Hall’s alumna who had been there a few years after me. I had never heard her name.

She had heard mine. Years earlier, older girls at the school had told her about me. She held on to my name, and when she went to a lawyer she remembered it. By then I had married and changed it, and they found me anyway.

I called Matt and asked. “Who is Melissa?” There was a pause long enough to hear him decide something, then a sigh, and then he told me he had had sex with Melissa while she was a student.

Here is what I did next, and I’d ask you to withhold judgment. I told him I would call the lawyer, find out what she had, and report back.

That’s what twenty-two years of being groomed looks like at a desk in Midtown. You don’t make a decision. The decision was made for you a long time ago, in a dorm room, and you’re simply carrying it out.

I did call the lawyer. And when I heard my own voice say “I’m not ready to talk to you, I want to talk to Melissa,” I think that was the first sentence in two decades that I said entirely for myself.

Melissa called that afternoon. I don’t remember how she started. I remember what I said before she got far.

“I’ve been waiting for your call for twenty years.”

I meant it literally. Some part of me had always known I wasn’t the only one. I just couldn’t go looking. I could only wait to be found.

Hilary Simon and Melissa Fares, photographed in Far Rockaway, New York, 2025.

She told me her story, and I heard my own memories come out of a stranger’s mouth. He called her “Little One.” He called me “Little One.” He took her to the same hotel in Northampton. He told her he would kill himself if she ever told anyone, which is a thing he had also told me, more than once, in nearly the same words. He had made himself the center of her emotional world before he ever touched her. He had a script.

For twenty years he had me believing that what happened was singular, and that it was my fault. By the end of that call it was a pattern, and I was a data point. I was not special. It is a strange thing to grieve, not being special to the person who hurt you. I grieved it anyway.

After more than three decades teaching at that school, he resigned the same day.

I arrived at Miss Hall’s, an all-girls boarding school in Pittsfield, Massachusetts, in the fall of 2001. I was fourteen, homesick, and like every other girl my age, positive I was more grown up than I was.

Rutledge had been teaching history there for a decade. He was a big man with a booming voice, married with two daughters. He lived with his family in a school-owned house across the street from the main entrance. He used to cut the lunch line announcing himself as “Mr. Wonderful.” Girls talked about him like he was a minor deity. They also mentioned, in the breezy way teenagers mention terrible things, that he had a type.

Some evenings, he was one of the adults who did bed checks in the dorms. The others always stood in the doorway. He came in and sat on the edge of my bed.

By the next fall he was my advisor and my cross-country coach. There was no door at that school he couldn’t open. On the long drives to meets, he told me to sit next to him in the school van. He called me his copilot. The rest of the team sat behind us. He would put his hand on my upper thigh, or pull me close until our legs were touching. I watched the Berkshire hills go by and tried not to look down.

That was the first line he crossed. I was fifteen. After that he crossed them one at a time until there were none left. He kept abusing me for years after I graduated.

From the outside, those years looked like a success story.

I went to college and then law school. I became a civil defense attorney. I got married. I had a son. I was good at my job.

I could find the unanswered email in ten thousand pages of discovery. The report nobody followed up on. I couldn’t open my own file.

When I tell this story, people ask me some version of the same question. How did nobody notice?

In the late 1990s, years before I ever set foot on Miss Hall’s campus, a student stood up at a school meeting and said Mr. Rutledge was having sex with another student. The school suspended her for the rest of the year, barred her from graduation and made her write him an apology letter. He kept teaching.

On my graduation day, Rutledge kissed me and told me that he loved me. A classmate told a staff member, who reported it to the administration. In a memo, Rutledge admitted telling me he loved me but said “[it was] not a romantic expression.” He denied the kiss. They took his word for it. No one called me or my parents.

A few years later, after a family reported that he had made advances toward their daughter, the head of school at that time, Jeannie Norris, put a warning to Rutledge in writing. “This isn’t the 70s or the 80s,” she wrote. “Society has no stomach for any kind of inappropriate behavior between adults and girls or teachers and students.” She was worried about the school’s reputation, and about his. In the letter she said the incident had “the potential for seriously damaging the School and your [Rutledge’s] reputation.” He was not fired.

Over the years that followed Rutledge was made chair of the history department and collected faculty honors. More than one person gave the school my name as a girl he had singled out. Nobody ever called me. In June 2023, I heard another alumna tried to raise concerns about him with the head of school at that time. He was still teaching nine months later, when Melissa reported him.

In August 2025 Miss Hall’s published the results of an outside investigation it had commissioned from Aleta Law. The investigators substantiated grooming and abuse by Rutledge involving at least five students. They found school leadership had been warned about him over the years and hadn’t acted. Staff members told investigators they had suspected him and kept quiet, some because they feared retaliation, others because they assumed no one in charge would listen.

It went beyond Rutledge. The investigation found that seven other Miss Hall’s employees had engaged in sexual misconduct with students, dating back to the 1940s. Eight adults across eighty plus years. That’s a culture of abuse.

A Berkshire County grand jury has since indicted Norris on a charge of reckless endangerment of a child. She has pleaded not guilty. Another former Miss Hall’s teacher has been indicted for assault with intent to rape and indecent assault and two counts battery of a student. He has also pleaded not guilty.

I read all sixty pages of the Aleta Law report in one sitting. Nothing in it surprised me. It still knocked the air out of me to see my adolescence reduced to numbered findings.

Melissa arrived at Miss Hall’s in 2007, two years after I left.

People sometimes call us friends. That’s true, but it’s a small word for it. I call her my sister survivor.

I wouldn’t be writing this if Melissa hadn’t gone first. She went to the school alone. In April 2024, she told her story publicly. A few weeks later, I told mine. Then other women came forward. They said Rutledge had abused them too.

In October 2024, the Berkshire district attorney said he didn’t believe he could charge Rutledge. In Massachusetts, the age of consent is sixteen. Under the law, a teacher could claim that a sixteen- or seventeen-year-old student had consented.

Melissa and I set out to change the law. We testified at the State House and knocked on every door that would open. Enough Abuse, a Massachusetts nonprofit, had been fighting for this for years. Two national advocacy groups, World Without Exploitation and I Have The Right To, stood with us. Representatives Leigh Davis and John Lawn pushed for it in the House, and Senator Joan Lovely added it to the state budget. In July, Governor Healey signed the Trusted Adults Act.

In Massachusetts, it is now a felony for a teacher or coach to have sex with a student under eighteen.

Melissa and I spoke at the signing ceremony. I stood right next to the governor and thought about the girl in the front seat of the school van, with her teacher’s hand on her leg.

While we were working on the law, Massachusetts State Police and a new team of prosecutors in the Berkshire district attorney’s office had reopened the investigation into Rutledge. Melissa and I testified before a grand jury. In March, he was indicted on three counts of rape.

In April, he was arraigned. It was the first time Melissa and I faced him together. In the courtroom, I handed out orange heart stickers. Orange is Melissa’s favorite color. When we saw Rutledge, we both went numb. We had learned to do that as girls, when going somewhere else in our heads was the only way through. He pleaded not guilty.

I looked back at the benches. They were full of orange. Teachers from Miss Hall’s, people from the community, alumnae across generations. I had been alone with this since I was fifteen. That day, a whole room sat behind us. Afterward, Melissa told reporters that for the first time, she held the power in a room with him. I felt it too.

This month, nine years after #MeToo took off, a jury in London convicted Russell Brand of one rape and three sexual assaults. A judge sentenced him to ten and a half years in prison. His crimes went back to 2004. Brand’s attorneys argued the women had waited too long to be believed. I waited twenty years. Delay is often the most ordinary fact in these cases.

In the midterms, Ohio elected Amy Acton governor. A few weeks before the vote, her opponent’s campaign ran an ad in which her estranged mother called her a liar. Acton’s stepfather had been charged with raping her when she was a child. Republicans and Democrats both condemned the ad. She won anyway.

I watched the returns on election night and thought about the girls at Miss Hall’s who told the truth and were called liars. Survivors get called liars all the time. We almost never get to watch one win.

Tarana Burke knew survivors weren’t being believed long before most people were listening. She started saying “me too” in 2006 to reach Black girls who had survived sexual violence, more than ten years before it became a hashtag. Every survivor who spoke after her made it a little easier for the next one.

In November 2024, a Cornell student told campus police and the Title IX office that she had been gang-raped at a fraternity house weeks earlier. No one has been charged. Cornell’s president set up a task force on sexual assault, but he later admitted he never checked how her case ended.

When I read that, I was back at Miss Hall’s on graduation day, waiting for a phone call that nobody made.

The Epstein survivors know that silence too. For decades, powerful people looked away. Last year survivors pushed Congress to pass a law requiring the Justice Department to release its Epstein files. Millions of pages came out. There have been no arrests in the United States.

I’m still hopeful. Survivors everywhere keep coming forward, and some of the people in charge are finally acting. My body knew what Rutledge had done to me long before I let myself say it aloud. I didn’t have the words. Survivors today do, and they have each other. Melissa found me.

The criminal case against Rutledge isn’t over. His lawyer has asked a judge to dismiss all charges. We don’t know yet whether there will be a trial. Whatever the judge decides, I’ve already reached my own verdict. I’m healing and Rutledge doesn’t get a say in that.

For most of my life, I carried shame that was never mine. He handed it to me. Every adult who looked away handed me a little more.

Predators don’t work alone. Someone always sees something. In the movie Spotlight, a lawyer says that if it takes a village to raise a child, it takes a village to abuse one. My village saw. The people in charge did nothing.

I’ve given the shame back. It belongs to him, and to the people who could have stopped him.

If you are a survivor and you are still carrying shame, you can put it down.

Borrow my courage if you need it. Melissa lent me hers.

Neither Matthew Rutledge nor Jean Norris responded to Vanity Fair for the original story, and neither of them has made direct statements to the press. Norris, through her attorney, claimed not to know that Rutledge abused students.

Over the years, Shonda Rhimes has been taking over television with dramas and romances that people can’t get enough of. Thanks to streaming, fans are able to rewatch and discover her projects. Scandal, for instance, is arguably one of Rhimes’ best shows, even eight years after its final season aired. Unfortunately, those streaming it with a Netflix subscription will soon have to say goodbye, meaning I have to say goodbye to one of my favorite TV couples, too.

For the second time since initially being added to Netflix back in 2014, Scandal is set to leave the streaming giant in December. This comes less than two years after the political drama rejoined Netflix in June 2025, five years after it originally left. Fans will have until December 17 to watch all seven seasons, and it’s unknown if Scandal will be added to Netflix again.

The reason for Scandal’s departure from Netflix likely has to do with the licensing agreement with the streamer expiring. However, it’s unknown if another deal will be made. It’s definitely disappointing, considering Scandal was one of the best shows on television, and soon, a lot of people won’t be able to watch it. Luckily, Netflix is not the only place to stream Scandal.

While the series is leaving Netflix in December, those with a Hulu subscription will have no problem catching up on Olivia Pope. All seven seasons are available to stream on the Disney-owned platform, and there’s no indication that it will be leaving. So fans will be able to catch all of Scandal’s biggest moments, and it means that I can still watch Olivia and Fitz.

I’m not one to wish for the downfall of a couple and root for an affair, but when it comes to Scandal, it’s kind of hard not to. Kerry Washington’s Olivia Pope and Tony Goldwyn’s President Fitzgerald “Fitz” Thomas Grant III were the couple on Scandal. They had a tumultuous relationship as they denied feelings for one another pretty early on, since Olivia had worked on Fitz’s campaign and was the White House Director of Communications. Not to mention the fact that Fitz was married to Melody “Mellie” Margaret Grant (Bellamy Young). He later divorced her, and she was thriving without him, so it definitely all worked out in the end.

However, with their secret sessions and sexual tension, as well as the fact that Fitz would have literally given the country to save Olivia when she was taken, their relationship was just too good to be an affair. No one was able to keep them apart. Of course, it wasn’t always easy, especially after their relationship and affair became public knowledge, but they always found their way back to each other.

Even today, Olitz remains a favorite with fans. The couple is still talked about online, with plenty of edits going around on TikTok. It helps that Washington and Goldwyn still have love for the series and their on-screen relationship as well. They’ve reunited on numerous occasions over the years, both for events and personally. Goldwyn has even shared his hope that Washington would appear on Law & Order, and she has shared that same sentiment. He admitted back in 2025 that he keeps “bugging her” about it, so maybe a reunion on another show could happen.

Plus, we'll always have Olivia and Fitz. Well, we won't always have them on Netflix, because Scandal is leaving on December 17. However, if you'd like to keep watching the show, you can stream it on Hulu too.

Passionate writer. Obsessed with anything and everything entertainment, specifically movies and television. Can get easily attached to fictional characters.

#3504. Apple engineers ‘actively working’ on Face ID for iPhone Duo 2’s outer display: report

Next fall, Apple will introduce its second-generation iPhone Duo. It’s unclear what it’ll offer in terms of meaningful upgrades outside of the usual chip upgrades and camera improvements, but Apple engineers are reportedly attempting to bake Face ID into the device. That said, the feature might not make the cutoff.

According to Bloomberg’s Mark Gurman, Apple has two priorities for iPhone Duo: Face ID and the Action Button. The latter might just end up being a new software addition to Camera Control that allows you to remap the hold action from Siri in Camera to an app of your choice.

As for Face ID, Apple engineers are ‘actively working’ on integrating the technology on the device, specifically on the outer display:

Other goals for the next couple of generations include adding a telephoto camera and making the device thinner and lighter overall. But Face ID is the top priority. I’m told that Apple has already developed prototypes of the iPhone Duo 2 with Face ID, and engineers are still actively working to integrate the facial-recognition system into the outer display of the second-generation model.

That said, the feature might not make it. According to Gurman, the timelines are tight here and it isn’t quite ready – so he isn’t reporting with certainty on whether or not this feature will make it. If it doesn’t debut with the iPhone Duo 2, it’ll likely be in the cards for iPhone Duo 3 in 2028.

Later down the road, the company wants to introduce an improved camera system for the iPhone Duo, including a telephoto camera. It also wants to make the device even thinner and lighter. The Duo definitely needs to be lighter, but making it even thinner would be an interesting feat.

While Face ID on the iPhone Duo would certainly be much appreciated, I’m not quite convinced that it’ll be super meaningful on only the outer display.

Being 8 years late to the foldable party, kinda makes you wonder why they weren't "actively working" on it during that time. They got it into the Air afterall.

If they magically make it happen for the Duo 2 then it looks like they held it back purposefully for yearly incremental improvement reasons as opposed to it not being possible.

I’m fine with Touch ID, but whenever it is bothersome, it’s usually on the inner display, where it can be hard to reach the button depending on how you’re holding the device. If I could only have Face ID on one display, I think I’d rather have it on the inner display.

Orientation can make a huge difference for how you reach Touch ID on the inner display, whereas you’re generally only going to hold the outer display one of two ways: upright in your left hand, or upright in your right hand.
