#3503. New Scientific Analysis Suggests Jeffrey Epstein Was Murdered. His Brother, For One, Feels Validated.

One day in August 2019, Mark Epstein was having breakfast at a Virginia hotel when he looked at the TV and saw CNN reporting that his older brother, Jeffrey Epstein, had died by suicide in a Manhattan federal prison. As jarring as the report was, he had no reason to doubt it.

“I knew he wouldn’t want to live the rest of his life in jail,” Mark told Vanity Fair this week. “He had no children to worry about. Our parents were gone. He knew he didn’t have to worry about me.”

Mark says he finished his omelet and headed back to New York. Then, like so many other Americans, he started to become skeptical of the official narrative.

Over the last seven years, the endless conspiracy theories surrounding Jeffrey Epstein’s death have largely been relegated to the backwaters of YouTube and Reddit, while local and federal authorities have stuck to the suicide story. But this week there was a breakthrough. On Monday, Michael Freeman, a leading forensic scientist who testified for the prosecution in the trial of Derek Chauvin for the murder of George Floyd, issued the most legitimate challenge to date to the prevailing consensus.

Freeman presented his findings at a historic London legal society, saying, “The pattern and distribution and multitude of injuries are not explained by a suicidal hanging.” In a New York Times story published the same day as the presentation, Freeman told the publication that he had no view on who might have killed Jeffrey: “All I’m interested in is, how did this get so sideways?” Along with several global news outlets, including CBS and the BBC, the paper covered the presentation with a straight face even as it noted that Freeman’s efforts to publish his findings in a peer-reviewed journal had thus far been rejected.

The relationship between Donald Trump and Jeffrey Epstein has loomed large over the president’s second term.

In his thick Brooklyn accent, Mark Epstein, who has long been trying to prove that his brother was murdered while awaiting trial on sex trafficking charges, excitedly recounted this new development over the phone the day after Freeman’s presentation, which he attended.

“This crosses all party lines,” Mark said. “Most people believe he didn’t commit suicide. So it’s a mystery. People want an answer to that. I think now they have the answer.”

Mark emphasized that the story of the recent findings was not about him but rather about his brother’s death and Freeman’s work. It was Freeman who reached out to him, Mark said, based on what the scientist independently thought was shoddy work on Jeffrey’s autopsy, and Mark agreed to turn over all the records, reports, and photographs he had as next of kin.

“I want to make it really clear,” he said. “I didn’t pay for this. He’s never asked me for anything other than the information, which I gave him willingly. And he’s been studying this. As a matter of fact, the night before last was the first time I ever met him face-to-face.”

Still, Mark has made his suspicions both his calling card and his personal mission in recent years. After working in real estate investing and serving as the chair of Cooper Union’s board of trustees, he had his own business dealings come under some scrutiny as Jeffrey’s life and crimes dominated political and cultural discourse beginning in the late 2010s—Jeffrey allegedly housed models and employees in an Upper East Side building that was predominantly owned by his brother’s real estate holding company. In the years since his brother’s death, Mark has said that Jeffrey “definitely had dirt” on Donald Trump, and he became a minor fixation amid the Epstein files rollout on account of emails containing banter between him and his brother. (Trump has denied any prior knowledge of Jeffrey’s crimes and said that the release of the Epstein files “totally exonerated” him.) Mark has dismissed a suicide note purportedly written by Jeffrey as a fabrication.

Jeffrey’s death certificate initially said “pending further study” in regard to the cause of death, rather than ruling it a homicide or suicide, but the chief medical examiner ruled it a suicide days later. “All the pathologists I’ve spoken to,” says Mark, “they said, [if] an initial death certificate says ‘pending further study,’ you don’t get an answer usually for weeks or more because something’s being studied.” Mark hired the celebrity forensic pathologist Michael Baden to observe and evaluate the autopsy, and Baden previously stated that “the evidence points to homicide.” Federal officials’ handling of the matter in the years to come only amplified Mark’s concern.

“You know a suicide when you see one,” FBI director Kash Patel said last year while he was under fire for not producing any proof of the Epstein conspiracies he had been touting during his time as a mere conservative podcast personality, “and that’s what that was.”

“I actually laughed out loud when I heard that,” Mark said, “because I thought, How many suicides has this fucking jackass actually seen?”

So who does Mark think killed his brother?

“It’s like in a Mob hit,” he said. “You try to find who the hit man was, and then you try to find who ordered the hit.” The hit man, he figured, could only be someone among a limited number of people: prison employees and other prisoners who had been on Jeffrey’s security tier. “Then the question becomes,” said Mark, “who would have the ability to orchestrate this in a federal prison, and who would have the ability to have the DOJ cover it up?” He couldn’t think of anyone besides Trump. (Trump has not been accused of any wrongdoing in connection to Jeffrey’s death; in a 2023 interview with Tucker Carlson, when asked whether Jeffrey could have been killed, he said, “Oh sure, it’s possible. I mean, I don’t really believe—I think he probably committed suicide.”)

I thought Mark and I had developed some rapport over the conversation, particularly after I mentioned that I’d attended the same Coney Island middle school where he and his brother had been students; I emphasized that I was trying to listen to him carefully and take him seriously. But there was a bit more rancor in his tone after I said it was still difficult to believe that the Department of Justice could have successfully covered up the murder of the most high-profile prisoner in the world.

“If you don’t think that after what I just told you,” Mark said, “then you, sir, are a fucking idiot also.”

There are so many A+ celebrity bromances, from Matt Damon and Ben Affleck to Ryan Reynolds and Hugh Jackman. Of course, when talking about such male friendships, Brad Pitt and George Clooney have to be mentioned as well. The two Oscar winners have been friends for years, and a hallmark of the relationship is that the two enjoy taking playful shots at each other. That recently continued during some red carpet interviews, and I’m so glad this trolling between the two prank war participants is still going strong.

Brad Pitt recently stepped out for the Los Angeles premiere of his latest 2026 movie schedule entry, The Further Mis-Adventures of Cliff Booth, where he spoke with ET. During the chat, the news outlet referenced some recent comments that Pitt’s longtime friend and frequent co-star made about his dance moves. Never one to let a joke go unanswered, Pitt humorously clapped back with a take on Clooney’s opinion. Watch Clooney share his initial comments and Pitt drop his rebuttal in the Instagram video below:

A post shared by Entertainment Tonight (@entertainmenttonight)

Spoken like two men who have a friendly rivalry of sorts, and this dynamic goes back quite a while. It was especially present when the pair worked together on the Ocean’s Trilogy, which began back in 2001. Since then, the two have kept their relationship playful, which has led to some great moments. Even earlier this year, Pitt – while promoting his canine-centric movie, Heart of the Beast – mused that a dog could’ve replaced Clooney in Ocean’s Eleven. That’s a great jab but, still, I love Clooney’s take on being able to outdance Pitt:

You know, he’s such a jealous man. In fact, I outdanced him on the dance floor.

Talk about shots fired! Of course, it’s not at all surprising that the F1 star wouldn’t let that humorous critique go unanswered:

I mean, some people live in delusion. What can you say? What are you going to do? You can’t help him.

Of course, the self-deprecating actor also clarified that he couldn’t say with certainty that he’d outdo Clooney. His point was that he doesn’t necessarily “take pride in [his] dancing.” Of course, while Pitt and Clooney may take pleasure in skewering each other from time to time, they do have a genuine friendship and seem to really enjoy being around each other. That playful dynamic was apparently present when they worked on their most recent movie together.

Many may remember that George Clooney and Brad Pitt worked together on 2024’s Wolfs (which is streamable with an Apple TV subscription). Reports indicate that their bromance was alive and well amid production and, while promoting the film, Pitt and Clooney spoke positively of the experience. The jokes were, of course, also flying, and the pair even threw a bit of playful shade at their Ocean’s co-stars during the press tour. And, if all goes accordingly, the pair and their co-stars will be back together again.

Ocean’s Fourteen is in the works, with the surviving cast members reportedly reprising their roles. George Clooney has spoken about the film, and his comments suggest that this won’t just be a legacy sequel cashing in on nostalgia. I look forward to seeing him and Brad Pitt share the screen again, and I also hope that we can look forward to many more years of them trolling each other.

#3501. Here’s one small change that could improve iPhone Duo’s unoptimized apps

iPhone Duo has been out for about 3 weeks now, and I’ve happily been using mine since launch day. Many people have made a big deal about the app situation, but I’d largely say most apps I rely on are updated for iOS 27.0 at least.

That said, a fair number of apps are still from iOS 26 and earlier, and those apps have letterboxing. In my time since trying the phone, I feel one quick adjustment could make the letterboxing a lot less of an issue.

Right now, on the home screen, iPhone Duo allows you to long press an app and open it in Split View. All iPhone Duo apps allow Split View, even if the developer hasn’t compiled it for iOS 27 or 27.1.

One of the beautiful things about iPhone Duo Split View is the fact that you don’t have to decide what you’re splitting right away. On the other half of the display, you’ll see your home screen, and you can later decide what app to open.

So, given the fact that a non iOS 27 app will only occupy around half of the inner display anyways, I feel like it’d make sense to have an option to open every non-optimized app in Split View by default – rather than needing to select it every time. Or, better yet, toggle certain apps to always open in Split View.

Certain apps, even if they’re optimized for iOS 27, don’t quite feel right spread across the wider inner display of iPhone Duo – so it’d be nice to always have them in a half split without needing to think about it.

This would be a small UX improvement that I feel would go a long way, so if Apple could implement this on iPhone Duo – it’d certainly help out the app situation. While they’re at it, it’d be nice to have Slide Over on the iPhone Duo, for when you want to quickly see a smaller app on top of your full screen app.

#3500. PlayStation Network Outage Hits On GTA 6 Release Day Eve

PS5 users are reporting widespread technical issues as GTA 6 rolls out

What happens when a potential 250 million people try logging into a server at the same time? Problems, that's what. Thursday, Nov. 19 is the official release day for Grand Theft Auto 6 on PlayStation 5 and Xbox Series X, and it appears Sony's platform, commonly known as PlayStation Network, is already buckling the day before under enormous demand for the world's most hyped game.

Many PS5 users tried to plan ahead by preloading the game starting on Nov. 10. Sony surely anticipated potential issues — the company has publicly treated GTA 6's release as if it were a first-party game — but that did little to prevent outages. Players around the world are facing messages like "Sony services are busy," "Too many failed connection attempts," or a mishmash of different errors. Though Sony's official status tracker currently lists the network as healthy, websites like Down Detector are seeing a sudden jump in reports related to the service. Most PS5 players say they're experiencing login issues with the PlayStation network, but there are also many reports of PSN server connection issues and update and download hiccups.

Whether you've seen codes like WS-116449-5, CE-34861-2, or WS-37505-0, they all point to the same thing: PlayStation's servers are facing serious strain.

GTA 6 is the follow-up to one of the most successful video games of all time, so the number of people trying to log in at once and download the game is likely massive. In the United States, it's the early afternoon — so many GTA fans probably just got off work and are all trying to do the same thing.

Though GTA 6 is not a multiplayer game that requires an online connection, players must download the title and its mandatory updates before they can enjoy it. This would have been the case even if GTA 6 had been printed on a disc — seemingly all major games require a day-one download for new patches or security reasons, like the recent PS5 jailbreak situation. This means that millions of people are trying to download hundreds of gigabytes of data at the same time, which was never going to end well.

There's no timeline for when PlayStation's servers might stabilize — and by extension, GTA 6 — but given the importance of this release, Sony are undoubtedly working on it.

Grand Theft Auto 6 officially launches on Nov. 19 on PlayStation 5 and Xbox Series X.

#3499. Lux Pascal, Sarah Pidgeon, Ella Rubin, and More Glammed Up for Chanel’s Watches and Fine Jewelry Dinner

“That is the highest compliment you could give anyone!” Lux Pascal says after I tell her she looks like Megan Draper from Mad Men. We’re at Chanel’s Watches and Fine Jewelry holiday dinner, held at Daniel Humm’s new eponymous restaurant, Humm, in the West Village. Pascal is in a ’60s black modish leather minidress that she’s paired with a cat eye. On her wrists are Chanel’s Première Galon watch and Coco Crush bracelets, which, like her rings and earrings, are all dotted with diamonds. As I look around, most of the celebrities dressed by the brand are wearing looks that show off their French fine accessories. Ella Rubin, the Gen Z star of the hit teen TV show Sterling Point, has upgraded a simple pair of vintage Levi’s with a sleek black-and-gold Première Ribbon watch and several diamond rings. This is not a night for hidden gems.

The Pierre Yovanovitch–designed restaurant is a verified New York power room at the moment: There’s Derek Blasberg talking to Sarah Pidgeon about books—War and Peace gets a name-check—and Architectural Digest’s Amy Astley in a corner with Metropolitan Museum of Art board member Robert Denning. Indrė Rockefeller is here, as is stylist Vanessa Traina. In a feat of fun seating arrangements, the Chanel team has sat Rubin next to another young Ella: Beatty, the recent star of Monster and daughter of Warren Beatty and Annette Bening. (Although, with all due respect to those lovely Ellas, the two neighbors I’d most like to eavesdrop on are Devon Lee Carlson and Jack Harlow.) At the bar I hear two fashion people gossiping about industry hiring rumors: “Lauren Sherman says there’s two people in the running,” they whisper about some gig. I think I know what they’re talking about, but not enough to print it.

Laura Love and Devon Lee Carlson on November 17, 2026, in New York City (Photo by Dimitrios Kambouris/WireImage)

Guests mill about because there’s much to mill about: Humm’s filled his restaurant with dozens of notable, site-specific artworks. Louise Bourgeois supplied 24 watercolor paintings, as well as a fantastical sterling silver cast of one of her sculptures, situated by the bar. (Tonight it’s serving mezcal sours with guava and an apple brandy highball.) Francesco Clemente painted not one, not two, but four celestial murals across two months, with motifs of abstract stars, animals, trains, and clocks. On the walls in the main dining room are 12 pigment drawings by Roni Horn. Then there’s all the work by Rashid Johnson: In the lounge—which for this event doubles as a red carpet—hangs his painting Untitled Homes. With Yovanovitch, he also built a custom host stand cast in aluminum and painted red. It’s so textural that you can see the fingerprints, and a number of guests gather around it as the maître d’ explains Johnson’s artistic process like he’s a docent at The Met.

Chanel has decorated the tables with long taper candles and arrangements of deep fuchsia peonies and burgundy garden roses. Waiters serve Humm’s signature everything caviar bagels. When I think about ordering something other than the chicken, a waiter tells me not to. He’s right.

At the end of the night, after most guests are a few glasses of red wine (or martinis) deep, Pidgeon herself grabs a microphone. The event, as it turns out, has a surprise performer: girlsweetvoiced. “She captures something that’s very honest,” Pidgeon says of the emerging singer-songwriter, who then belts out a cover of Joni Mitchell’s “California.” Title aside, it’s been a very New York night.

The hype is real, but what about a movie?

The hype surrounding the long-awaited release of Grand Theft Auto VI has reached a fevered pitch, with reviews for the game universally saying it’s living up to that hype. The GTA series has consistently been one of the most popular gaming franchises of all time, and one of the most successful entertainment franchises on Earth. It’s also one of the only monster franchises that hasn’t been adapted as a movie or a TV show.

That’s always surprised me, because it seems ripe for a video game adaptation, right? Now, the CEO of Take-Two Interactive, the company that owns Rockstar, the studio that produces the games, was recently asked about a possible adaptation. His answer is actually kind of positive news, though hardly concrete evidence that an adaptation is on the way.

While appearing on The David Rubenstein Show, CEO Strauss Zelnick was asked about the possibility of a movie. He responded:

We're very careful about line extensions because this is a creative company, and our goal is to make the best entertainment on Earth.  Entertainment we’re always proud of. We would make a movie or a television show based on our intellectual property if our creative teams were passionate about it, if they thought that would somehow engage and delight our consumers. It's a high bar to do that, and, of course, there's always a risk of failure. So we don't rule it out, but we're very, very selective.

“Line extensions” are when business use existing products or intellectual property to expand how they can take advantage of markets, like, for example, video game movie adaptations. Take-Two, as Zelnick points out, has been very careful with how they’ve expanded their brands outside of video games. No franchise shows that more than GTA. It seems ripe for adaptation and really has been for decades, but they have yet to pull the trigger. They do seem open to it, though.

Like millions of other people, I’m still waiting for a few more hours to be able to play GTA VI, as we all have been for years now. Based on the glowing reviews, this could be the version of the game most likely to get adapted into a movie. Reviews have talked about the storyline in the new game, praising it for how well the story is incorporated into the game. It seems full of drama (and great music). Plus, there are two playable protagonists, a couple named Jason and Lucia.

This is the first time GTA has featured a female playable character, and it tells the story of the two, which to me sounds like the perfect basis for a possible film. While the characters in previous versions have been fun, these two actually sound like the most realistic characters, with a deep backstory together. That really leaves the option open.

It’s also worth mentioning that Zelnick, who took over Take-Two in 2007, has a history in the movie world as the former President of 20th Century Fox and overseeing hit movies like Home Alone and before that worked for Columbia Pictures Television. If anyone knows how to strike a good deal for Take-Two, it’s Zelnick. I would love to see it happen one day!

Obsession is that one film on the 2026 movie schedule that we can’t stop talking about, and why would we want to? Now we can stream it to our heart's content with a Netflix subscription, I needed to dig up all the fun behind-the-scenes facts I learned from writer/director Curry Barker. Each of these made me think of the movie in a whole different way! Let’s get into it. (SPOILERS ahead.)

I’m always curious about how movies change over time, and Barker told CinemaBlend about one pivotal scene that he played around with a lot. The writer/director was also the movie’s editor on the $750k independent production, and he told us about one exchange he tried a bunch of different ways . In his words:

The scene where they’re driving and she’s talking about romance and love. And she’s saying, like, ‘Hey, you know, you’re the only person I can talk to about this stuff.’ That scene changed so much. There’s probably like ten different versions of that scene. One that’s a little longer, one that’s shorter, one where she doesn’t even say the line, one where she goes into a longer thing. Like, I don’t know why. That scene just has so many different versions of it.

This sort of blew my mind because this is the scene I was playing over and over in my head after seeing the movie. It’s an important scene because it establishes Bear and Nikki’s relationship before Nikki loses her autonomy. Watching that scene made me wonder if Bear could have had a shot with Nikki if he had simply asked her out rather than using the One Wish Willow. With that in mind, I totally see why this scene would have needed tweaking, but I think it's perfect now.

When I first watched Obsession, I felt a chill down my spine when Bear called the number on the back of the One Wish Willow box. Then, I subsequently had so many questions about what was going on! When I talked to Barker about this scene, he revealed he was the one on the other side of the line.

Well, that was me… yeah, that’s my voice. He works for the One Wish Willow Company, he kind of answers their phone calls. He handles all the complaints of all the wishes. But, there’s no, I mean, I like to keep it pretty vague. I think you could think of it as some sort of purgatory that [Nikki’s] being kept in, right?

What a fun cameo! I had no idea Barker was the voice, but it’s a fun little tidbit I’ll always think about when I watch that scene. He gave us some interesting insight about what’s going on with that phone call, too. I'm never forgetting Nikki's screams on the other line.

One more BTS detail I want to share has to do with what didn’t make it into the film. Obsession really goes hard in the paint on the movie rating scale, so I was curious if there was a scene the director had to remove because it went too far. The answer is, yes, there was one moment.

There was only one thing I had to take out because it was too far, but other than that they really let me do whatever they wanted. And, I was kind of, like, shocked. This movie really felt like a bunch of kids getting together and making something, and hoping that the parents don’t come home. They never did. Nobody ever stopped us, and we just kept making the thing we wanted to make. Like, even the way we shot it. We thought someone was going to tell us to turn the lights on.

So, what was that “one thing”? During a Q&A (via Deadline), Barker revealed it was the scene where Nikki kills Sarah by smashing her head into the steering wheel. Barker said there was originally “about six or seven more smashes." The MPA ratings board was going to give the movie a NC-17 rating because of it. At first, Barker wasn’t happy about making the change, but when he saw the movie with an audience (and heard their reactions), he realized the number they landed on was “the right number” to choose.

You can check out the rest of our Obsession interview on CinemaBlend's YouTube. There we also talked about that gross cat scene and what probably happens after the ending. I know I’m always finding new theories online. Obsession really is the movie of the year for this horror fan, and I loved learning these behind-the-scenes facts.

#3495. Robert Pattinson Is the New James Bond—Revisit 007’s Style Legacy Here

There must be no male character across film history who has done more for menswear—and for the suit—than Bond, James Bond.

That is in part because the sartorial premise of Bond, the suave British spy, is remarkably simple: Presumably, all it takes to embody 007 is a black tuxedo, a sexy watch, and a pair of well-buffed dress shoes. And yet, as Daniel Craig, Pierce Brosnan, Sean Connery, and other dangerously handsome men have proven, a mere suit does not a 007 make. This is why, despite Bond being one of the most popular film characters of all time, you will rarely see ordinary men dare to take him on as a Halloween costume. There’s simply more to making Bond than a good tux.

Denis Villeneuve is set to direct the next era of the franchise, now under the creative control of Amazon MGM, and Robert Pattinson has been chosen to reincarnate the character conceived by Ian Fleming in 1953. In the announcement clip for Pattinson’s casting, the actor looks the part in a black tuxedo and white shirt, but it’s his eyes, which pierce through the camera rather than down the barrel of his gun, that do most of the talking and offer a suggestion of what Pattinson’s Bond may have to offer. Will he be a little darker and tortured, like his take on Batman? Or perhaps his Bond will be louche and somewhat pricklier.

A safer bet to make is that he will look good. One of the most enduring legacies of the James Bond franchise is how stylish both the character of Bond and the universe built around him have always been. Bond has appeared classic and timeless in style during each of the franchise’s eras, but hindsight offers a much richer perspective.

Pierce Brosnan, The World Is Not Enough, 1999.

As portrayed through the decades in the property’s famous title sequence, Bond is a silhouette—a classic, timeless silhouette. Fleming established the look in his development of the character when he made the suit his primary uniform. But it is Terence Young, the director of the first 007 films, who is responsible for the visual definition of Bond.

When Connery was cast as Bond for the first film, Dr. No (1962), Young, an avid wearer of suits himself, took him to his own tailor, Anthony Sinclair. We can credit Sinclair with developing the original silver screen Bond look: The suit was lighter in fit and tailoring than most other English suits at the time. The Bond suit had a soft shoulder and waist, but a strong, wide chest and a low button stance that elongated its wearer. Every Bond suit that’s followed has been measured to the standard of Sinclair’s work, and every Bond actor has had to compete with Connery’s charisma while wearing it.

Brosnan and his Brioni suits were indicative of the 1990s corporate look of the time. Craig wore Brioni too, but only for Casino Royale; Tom Ford created his subsequent suiting, which often stood out for the slim fit popular in the 2010s. Most memorable sartorially is Roger Moore’s take through the ’70s and ’80s, which often deviated from the sleekness that had come to define Bond by creating a little frisson with lighter, brighter fabrics and a bolder sense of playfulness.

The character of Bond, and the actor personifying him at a given time, have also become representative of a certain male standard: Connery in the ’60s, tan and athletic, or Brosnan in the ’90s, polished with lithe elegance. And then came Craig, whose casting was met with skepticism, to put it lightly. His arrival was marked by the image of the actor walking out of the ocean in tight swim trunks in Casino Royale. His strong legs, rounded shoulders, and sculpted, hairless chest cemented then and there the idea of what a leading man had become and would look like for the next two decades.

Daniel Craig as James Bond, Casino Royale, 2006.

Also synonymous with Bond are his watch and many vehicles. Most recently, Bond cars have all been made by Aston Martin, though Brosnan drove some spectacular BMWs. The official Bond timepiece since Brosnan’s turn has been Omega. But before such kinds of commercial partnerships were commonplace in Hollywood, Connery wore watches by Rolex, Gruen, and Breitling, while Moore wore pieces by Seiko.

With the news that Pattinson is taking on the mantle, an equally pressing question emerges: Who will be the first new Bond girl?

Some of the most memorable moments in the franchise’s history have been anchored by women. Halle Berry’s emergence from the ocean in an orange bikini and a white belt safekeeping a knife was only made better by the fact that this moment was an homage to the first Bond girl, Ursula Andress, and her ivory two-piece featuring a belt for her own weapon. Then there was Eva Green as Vesper Lynd in a slinky Versace dress in Casino Royale. But it didn’t get better than Grace Jones in A View to a Kill. As May Day, a fabulous femme fatale, Jones wore costumes designed for her by Azzedine Alaïa. How could anyone measure up?

Halle Berry and Pierce Brosnan, Die Another Day, 2002.

Roger Moore and Grace Jones, 1985, A View To a Kill, 1985.

Of course, we will have to see how stylistic choices play out in the 26th Bond film, which, like Bond movies of the past, will become emblematic of the era in which we live. It will also, as a creative project, have to contend with the way Hollywood operates today. The fact that Amazon now has full creative control over the franchise—the company acquired MGM, a co-owner of the Bond franchise rights, for $8.45 billion in 2022 and later struck a deal with the other co-owners in regard to creative authority—is the primary indication of that.

Pattinson will also be the first Bond with airtight fashion-brand deals. Craig was an Omega ambassador as an extension of his role as Bond, which made him a household name, and the 007s who came before him operated within a film industry that was not as closely connected to fashion.

Also unlike his predecessors, Pattinson is stepping into the role as a bona fide movie star who has appeared in three other major franchises (Harry Potter, Twilight, and Batman). He’s already one of the most prolific and bankable stars of his generation, and an undeniable part of being a movie star today is becoming the face of a franchise, a brand, or a product.

In September, Pattinson was announced as a global ambassador for Jaeger-LeCoultre, a Swiss watchmaker. But 007 has worn Omega watches onscreen for decades, a partnership between the brand and the franchise that dates back to the Brosnan years. If Omega’s partnership with the franchise remains for this new installment, it could present a potential conflict if Pattinson’s contract with Jaeger stipulates that he is not allowed to wear another brand’s watch onscreen or front related campaigns for competitors. It may sound like a banal preoccupation, as Pattinson has only just been cast, but there are millions of dollars at play, and actors today often make as much money from brand deals as they do from their turns onscreen.

Pattinson has also been an ambassador for Dior since 2013, serving first as a fragrance ambassador and subsequently as a face for ready-to-wear Dior Homme; he was originally tapped under Kris Van Assche, with his ambassadorship extending through Kim Jones’s tenure at the renamed Dior Men and now continuing with Jonathan Anderson at the helm of the French mega-brand. Will Anderson be providing his suits? The Irish designer has costumed films before, working with Luca Guadagnino on Challengers, Queer, and the upcoming Artificial. To design for the big screen would hardly be a stretch for him.

The real question is more existential: Should Bond wear high fashion? To return to the idea of the 007 silhouette, that in itself is counterintuitive to Pattinson saving the world in one of Anderson’s menswear takes on the famous Dior Bar jacket, with its nipped waist and slightly flared hem. And yet in this brave new world of brand deals, anything is possible.

#3494. Apple provides a safe way to ask an AI questions about your health

This is actually one of Apple’s research studies, but those volunteering to take part in it will be able to ask health questions – with three key assurances not guaranteed by other AI chatbots …

Apple launched its Research app back in 2019 with the goal of allowing customers to help universities and medical institutions with health studies. You typically agree to share certain anonymized information from the Apple Health app in order to provide data that can advance medical research. You may also be asked to complete questionnaires.

The Apple Health AI Usage Study is one of these, but it works in a somewhat different way. You’ll still be invited to share some of your health data, but will also be able to ask an AI system questions about your health.

When you ask health questions of a typical AI chatbot, you don’t know how reliable those answers may be or what will happen to your data. Apple study offers three assurances:

Apple says that answers will be generated by the same platform used by healthcare professionals.

The study is conducted in collaboration with OpenEvidence, a leading clinical AI platform widely used by healthcare professionals that generates answers using medical information from established sources such as The New England Journal of Medicine, Journal of the American Medical Association, and Nature.

The answers provided to you will include links to peer-reviewed clinical citations.

CNET reports on Apple’s assurance that none of your chats will be retained.

OpenEvidence will delete both question and response data within 24 hours. A small group of Apple researchers will have access to coded versions of survey responses, separated from personally identifiable information, summaries of conversations and categories of the most common conversation types.

Access to the study is currently limited to users in the US by downloading the app. If you try it, please do share your thoughts in the comments.

#3493. How To Watch The Social Reckoning At Home

"The Social Reckoning" is finally hitting the home market. It will become available to buy or rent on digital starting November 24, 2026, prior to its physical media release on January 12, 2027.

In case you're unfamiliar with "The Social Reckoning" writ large, here's the gist. Almost two decades after he won an Academy Award for writing the screenplay for "The Social Network," a 2010 dramatization of the founding of Facebook directed by David Fincher, Aaron Sorkin decided to make a sequel that focuses on what Facebook has become in the 2020s. Jesse Eisenberg, who earned an Oscar nod for playing Facebook founder Mark Zuckerberg in "The Social Network," declined to return to the role and was replaced by "Succession" veteran, Emmy and Tony winner, and Sorkin's "The Trial of the Chicago 7" collaborator Jeremy Strong. With Mikey Madison, Jeremy Allen White, Bill Burr, Wunmi Mosaku, Betty Gilpin, and Billy Magnussen starring alongside Strong, the project seemed almost too big to fail before it premiered in theaters on October 9, 2026.

Fail it did, though. Though it reportedly only lost a couple million for Sony (per Deadline), the film absolutely underperformed at the box office, and its rating on Rotten Tomatoes is a middling-to-bleak 54%. So what happened here? Well, from my perspective, "The Social Reckoning" is just a bad movie ... and /Film's chief film critic Chris Evangelista agrees with me. What went wrong as Sorkin tried to make a legacy sequel to one of the best films of the 21st century? Quite a lot actually!

I'll circle back to the "Social Network" of it all shortly, but the bottom line here is that "The Social Reckoning" just ... stinks to high heaven. From the embarrassing prologue featuring Portia Doubleday as a caricature named Kayleigh (I'm not kidding) to the fact that Aaron Sorkin keeps forcing Oscar winner Mikey Madison into outfits that would make her title character from "Anora" blush (in the name of corporate espionage), I found "The Social Network" to be a uniformly dreadful watch from start to finish. Not only is the script clunky as all hell — unfortunately, an ongoing problem with many of Sorkin's recent screenplays — but the story is attempting to make some sort of larger point that doesn't just fall flat but thuds directly to the floor. We already know social media makes everyone angry and insane, and we also know that social media has contributed to right-wing radicalization. Sorkin making a movie that beats us over the head with these two ideas and also ends in a full recreation of the January 6, 2021 insurrection is just as bad as it sounds in theory.

It's also incredible to me that Sorkin managed to cast a lot of great actors and coach them into giving some of the worst performances of their careers. Madison is an enigmatic and compelling performer, and Sorkin transforms her into the robotic Facebook whistleblower Frances Haugen, a deeply unlikable person who doesn't seem to understand human behavior. Jeremy Allen White's journalist Jeff Horwitz is nothing but an exposition machine, and Jeremy Strong's Mark Zuckerberg has no interiority and sounds like Kermit the Frog. The only person who's good in this movie is Bill Burr. Think about that for a second.

"The Social Network" might be one of my very favorite movies of all time, but I can tell you, from a completely unbiased perspective, that "The Social Reckoning" is a wholly undeserving sequel to that 2010 masterpiece. It's clear now, with plenty of hindsight and movies like this, that "The Social Network" was good because of director David Fincher and despite Sorkin. To be fair to Sorkin, he basically admitted that to The Hollywood Reporter after "The Social Reckoning" got soundly panned.

"I would have rather David Fincher directed it — I would rather David Fincher direct everything — but David has an exclusive deal at Netflix, and this was owned by Sony," Sorkin told the outlet on their "Awards Chatter" podcast. Not only did Sorkin also admit that he's "very worried that the parts of directing that [he's] not good at are those parts that you can't learn," he also said, "I was surprised by how little of the science of filmmaking I'd managed to absorb [from other directors] ... I have no visual sensibility, it turns out."

I have to agree with him. Despite the same cinematographer — Jeff Cronenweth — working on both "Network" and "Reckoning," the sequel is visually bland, unimaginatively shot, and even recycles a couple reaction and establishing shots throughout its run time. Basically, "The Social Reckoning" is a poorly made film that I cannot in good conscience recommend; in fact, I'd recommend you just watch "The Social Network" instead. But if you're still interested, you can check out "The Social Reckoning" at home once it's available.

One of the best SNL sketches in years is producing some strong reactions.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

The goal of sharing a Saturday Night Live sketch is typically to elicit a laugh, but now and again, one makes such a thoughtful or important point that people use it as a conversation starter or as evidence to prove a point. That’s exactly what’s going on with last weekend’s Sister sketch, a fake commercial about how caregiving responsibilities overwhelmingly fall on the women in the family. Tens of thousands have taken to social media to share or retweet the sketch alongside comments about how they feel seen, and now, we’ve reached the point where people are using it to call out their own family members.

Sister has been watched more than five million times in the past few days on YouTube, more than twenty million times on X and untold millions of times more on additional social platforms. If you look at comments on any of these platforms, two immediate themes jump out. Many people are saying they feel exactly like the title sister in the sketch, and many others are calling out family members for not helping with caregiving responsibilities.

Actually, I probably phrased that second one too nicely. What many people are doing is throwing up their middle fingers at family members and telling stories about their avoidance and/ or woeful incompetence. Here’s a story with more than 69,000 likes…

My mom literally called me to come over to help her water a single outdoor plant, and when I got there she was cooking for my older brother who had been there the entire time.

That wild story is definitely not an outlier either. The angry rants are just pouring out of people, an overwhelming majority of whom are women who feel like they are left doing everything while their siblings live their lives. Some are mad about how they did everything until their parent died, only to find out their absentee sibling(s) got the exact same inheritance. Others are mad about how their family members infrequently show up and then critique the job they were doing and question the decisions they make.

One woman shared that a caretaker in her family was later sued by the surviving family members for taking money out of the disabled parent’s bank account to buy said parent food and medicine. You can check out that banger below, which has about five thousand likes…

With Sister you can also wait for her to spend your dad’s money on essentials for him like groceries or clothes and then sue her later - because she never had financial power of attorney!

Seriously, don’t take my word for it. Look wherever the Sister sketch is embedded. You’ll immediately start running into story after story of angry people who need to let it out. I saw one woman calling out the parent they’re looking after for raising her brother to think he didn’t need to help. I’ve seen numerous lawyers, nurses, dementia care workers and doctors saying they see the same dynamic over and over again. I saw one woman say her brother who lives near her mom can’t be bothered to help; so, she has to travel across the country to handle things.

watching this from my mom’s house 1500 miles away bc my brother Just Can’t Manage to get her to the doctor or the dentist. he lives down the street

It’s clear this sketch, which is filled with fun little easter eggs, struck a nerve, but it seems like in a very therapeutic way. It’s allowing people to give voice to frustrations they’ve clearly had for a long time, and if it leads to even some family members doing a little self-reflecting and helping out a bit more, it’ll be a huge victory. #3491. The 10 greatest games to never get a GOTY nomination

The Game Awards announced its 2026 nominations yesterday, though not without controversy. Grand Theft Auto 6 — a game that isn't even out yet — leads the pack with eight nominations, including Game of the Year. No indies managed to get a GOTY nomination this year, despite the release of acclaimed games like Mina the Hollower and Big Walk. Several blockbusters — including Polygon favorites like Fire Emblem: Fortune's Weave and Pokémon Pokopia — were also snubbed for the night's biggest award.

While there's a lot to be said about 2026's Game Awards snubs, some of the greatest games of all time never received a GOTY nomination. While the games below may have been nominated (or won) in other Game Awards categories, they never got their fair shot at Game of the Year honors.

Where to play: PlayStation 4, Windows PC, Xbox One

Dark Souls 3 was a gorgeous, somber conclusion to FromSoftware's groundbreaking Dark Souls trilogy. By speeding up the pace of combat, Dark Souls 3 bridged Bloodborne and Elden Ring, streamlining an already iconic gameplay loop. To close out its trilogy, FromSoft proved it had complete mastery over the gameplay style it innovated years earlier.

Despite widespread acclaim, Dark Souls 3 was not nominated for Game of the Year in 2016, only getting a nod for Best RPG. Fans should take comfort in the fact that 2016 was an absolutely stacked year, though, with Overwatch, Doom, and Inside all competing for top honors. There's also the fact that very difficult games face an uphill battle in the GOTY race.

Where to play: Nintendo Switch, PlayStation 4, Windows PC, Xbox One

Outer Wilds is hard to categorize. At once an open-world explorer, an action adventure title, and a puzzle game, it dropped a traditional combat focus in favor of rewarding curiosity and knowledge. Couple that with a tightly written story, and you have one of the most immersive, combat-free gaming experiences of the decade.

Outer Wilds faced even stiffer competition than Dark Souls 3. 2019 was a competitive year, with Control, Death Stranding, Sekiro: Shadows Die Twice, Super Smash Bros. Ultimate, The Outer Worlds, and the Resident Evil 2 remake fighting for top honors. Several other great games, like Disco Elysium, Fire Emblem: Three Houses, and Star Wars Jedi: Fallen Order also failed to secure nominations. So, for an indie game — which tend to build popularity via word of mouth — Outer Wilds was always a deserving but unlikely nomination.

Where to play: Nintendo Switch, PlayStation 4, Windows PC, Xbox One

NieR:Automata this relatively obscure spin-off of Square Enix's Drakengard series to mainstream audiences. Its intricate, existential story and seamless transitions between bullet-hell, hack-and-slash, and side-scrolling gameplay left a mark on millions of gamers worldwide.

Automata lost the nomination race to games like Breath of the Wild, Super Mario Odyssey, and Horizon Zero Dawn — games with enormous mainstream appeal. Though Automata was a breakout critical and commercial success for its franchise, it still came from a relatively niche series. What's more, the game's heavy philosophical themes and dozens of endings may have been a bit opaque for voters.

Ghost of Yotei, the highly anticipated follow-up to 2020 GOTY nominee Ghost of Tsushima, is about as cinematic as a game can get. With influence from filmmakers like Takashi Miike (13 Assassins) and Shinichiro Watanabe (Cowboy Bebop), Ghost of Yotei even has a game mode inspired by the work of Seven Samurai director Akira Kurosawa. And, it shows off its stunning graphics and cinematic influences without compromising on fluid, intense gameplay.

Ghost of Yotei earned seven Game Awards nominations in 2025, including Best Direction, Narrative, Audio Design, Action/Adventure Game, and more. So many people were confused about how a game that, apparently had some of the best direction, design, action gameplay and storytelling of the year could miss out on a GOTY nomination. Polygon's Oli Welsh even said "you could have grown it in a lab to win Game of the Year." Unfortunately, Ghost of Yotei paid a sequel tax — critics thought it didn't distinguish itself from Ghost of Tsushima quite enough.

Donkey Kong Country: Tropical Freeze deserved better. It's an absolute masterclass in platformer design, with carefully themed levels and gimmicks that feel purposeful. Developers mastered a sense of momentum, getting players to chain satisfying rolls, jumps, and precise landings. Also, everything is set to an absolutely classic soundtrack by composer David Wise.

Tropical Freeze came out in 2014, the first year of the Game Awards, alongside titles like Bayonetta 2, Dark Souls 2, and Dragon Age: Inquisition. So, it didn't quite fit in with the kind of vibe the early Game Awards honored. Also, Tropical Freeze was initially a Wii U game. While a Nintendo Switch port has brought the game to platformer fans nationwide, the commercial failures of the Wii U hindered its success.

Where to play: Nintendo Switch, PlayStation 4, Windows PC, Xbox One

Considered one of the best games of the 2010s, Hollow Knight dropped players into a vast, rich world with minimal guidance. Since 2017, millions of gamers have uncovered Hallownest's secrets, pieced together its tragic history, and died a lot. (It's a hard game!)

Hollow Knight didn't make a ton of headlines when it first came out. Like many other indie titles, it spread slowly via word of mouth. So, it lacked the kind of blockbuster momentum that can propel a game to a GOTY nod. Hollow Knight received an indirect nod last year through the nomination of its sequel Hollow Knight: Silksong, which lost out to Clair Obscur: Expedition 33.

Where to play: PlayStation 4, Windows PC, Xbox One

Konami and Bloober Team's Silent Hill 2 revisits one of the greatest psychological horror games of all time. It faithfully recreated the suffocating atmosphere and emotional weight of the 2001 original, while upgrading its gameplay to modern survival horror standards. Stronger performances and updated graphics made the terror and tragedy of Silent Hill 2 accessible to a new generation of gamers.

But horror games can be a tough sell at The Game Awards. Though high-profile blockbusters like Resident Evil 2 have been nominated, the only horror-adjacent game to bring home GOTY was The Last of Us Part II in 2020. Silent Hill 2 was also a remake; remakes are rarely nominated and have never won GOTY.

Fire Emblem: Three Houses was the best-selling mainline Fire Emblem game of all time, catapulting the series into Nintendo flagship status. Its iconic route split drew players into an intricate tale of war, love, and betrayal. It also sparked years upon years of discourse and fan arguments, which continue to this day. That ought to count for something.

Like Outer Wilds, Three Houses faced stiff competition amid a stacked 2019 gaming lineup. Also, Three Houses was a bit rough around the edges, particularly graphically. Couple that with a monastery hub that can feel repetitive (and the fact that you need to play the game four times to get the full story), and it's easy to understand why Three Houses failed to secure a GOTY nomination. That doesn't make it hurt less, though.

Where to play: Nintendo Switch 2, PlayStation 4, Windows PC, Xbox One

Yakuza 0 took on a lot. It features two protagonists, a high-stakes crime drama, over-the-top combat, and a quirky sense of humor, all without losing the series' integral "cool factor." It succeeded with flying colors, telling an emotional story about two iconic characters while leaving room for an all-important disco mini game.

When it was released overseas in 2016, Yakuza 0 was hampered by what Parasite director Bong Joon Ho called "the one-inch tall barrier of subtitles." Without an English dub upon release (it would eventually get one via its 2025 Director's Cut release), Yakuza 0's viral popularity was a slow burn with Western audiences. Once it launched on Steam in 2018, Yakuza 0 nearly doubled its past sales, and is now the best-selling game in the series. It may be the game that inspired a thousand memes — and took the Yakuza series into the mainstream — but it wasn't an overnight blockbuster.

Where to play: Nintendo Switch, PlayStation 5, Windows PC, Xbox Series X

Of course, this list would not be complete without Mina the Hollower, one of the most baffling GOTY nomination snubs of this year. Its intricately designed levels took an insane amount of effort, rivaling any AAA game out right now. That effort resulted in one of the year's best games, a loving homage to early Zelda games, the Game Boy Color, and Gothic horror.

While it received a nod for best indie game, Mina the Hollower was left off an indie-free GOTY nomination list. Though it was, critically speaking, one of the best received games of the year, it looks as though The Game Awards voters focused on mainstream blockbusters this year. It's also very, very hard, which may have dulled its mass appeal.

What’s in pole position for gaming’s top prize? Let’s make some predictions

#3490. Video podcasts coming soon to Apple TV and other devices

Apple will soon be adding a video podcasts section to Apple TV, which will also be available in the Apple TV app on other devices like smart TVs. That means it will come to more than a billion devices in total.

Access to the video podcasts will be free, with no requirement for an Apple TV subscription. Testing begins today, with the full rollout promised “soon” …

Apple shared the news with The New York Times.

On Monday, Apple will add a video podcasts section to Apple TV, initially just for testing with developers. They will soon be free to all users […] Apple also plans to increase the number of video podcasts on its regular Podcasts app.

The company says the move will benefit creators and listeners alike.

“We want podcasts to be available wherever people want to enjoy them — the small screens, big screens,” said Oliver Schusser, a vice president at Apple who oversees services including podcasts, television and music. “It’s really about discovery and helping the creators to reach a new audience. We didn’t approach this in a way that would financially benefit us.”

While podcasts began as audio only, it’s become increasingly common in recent years for them to be released as video also. This expands the reach to video platforms like YouTube, Hulu, and Netflix. Creators have welcomed Apple’s latest move, even if some are a little sad about what it says about the medium.

“It’s so helpful that people can go on their phones, they see a clip on Instagram, TikTok or Twitter and open the Apple app and now watch it on video,” he said. “People are already on their iPhones and they’re used to watching videos on their phones so it was the next logical step” […]

“Everything is TV now, which is a little bit heartbreaking for a lifelong audio person to say,” Ms. Martin of NPR said.

No date has yet been announced for the public rollout.

#3489. Cillian Murphy's 28 Years Later: Part III Will Only Happen Under One Condition, Says Director Danny Boyle

Are we going to see "28 Years Later: Part III?" Director Danny Boyle is certainly interested in doing it and Alex Garland has written a script. The problem? Money. This year's "28 Years Later: The Bone Temple" finally delivered the moment fans have been waiting for, bringing back Cillian Murphy as Jim. It was a small appearance teeing up something much larger in a presumed third installment. As Boyle recently explained, that movie is only going to happen if they can find the money.

Speaking recently with Deadline during an event for his new movie "Ink," Boyle's tabloid media origin story that will make you feel sick, the Oscar-winning director addressed the status of the third and presumably final entry in the "28" franchise. "There is a plan for a third part of '28 Years Later.' Alex has written a fantastic script," Boyle said. "We gotta raise the money to make it."

Sony Pictures produced both "28 Years Later" and "The Bone Temple." And while "28 Years Later" killed it at the box office, the sequel didn't. That's why Sony isn't eager to give it the green light. Speaking further, Boyle said that the third installment would bring the whole franchise to a close:

"[Cillian Murphy]'s up for it, and it's a fantastic part. Alex has written this fantastic part for him. Those of you who saw 'The Bone Temple,' the second part to '28 Years Later,' he's teased at the end of that. The third film does complete the story in a beautiful, mathematically perfect way, in which the circle is closed."

Creatively speaking, critics and audiences generally agreed that both of the recent "28" movies were damn good. But Hollywood is a business and money became an issue pretty quickly. "28 Years Later" made $151 million against a budget in the $60 million range. That was good enough. "28 Years Later: The Bone Temple" flopped at the box office though, bringing in just $58.5 million worldwide on a similar budget. Unfortunately, the math doesn't math for anyone who wants to make money in this business.

That's why "28 Years Later: Part III" probably won't happen. Admittedly, "probably" is doing some heavy lifting there. Cillian Murphy is an Oscar-winning actor for his work in "Oppenheimer," Danny Boyle is an Oscar-winning director, and Alex Garland is an Oscar-nominated screenwriter. It's a powerhouse team. That makes it unlikely but not impossible.

The most realistic path to getting it made would be partnering with a streaming service. Netflix is releasing Boyle's new movie "Ink" and the streamer also has a partnership with Sony. That would be the logical choice. But if Boyle and Garland want it as a more traditional theatrical release? That's where it gets more complicated and far less likely.

As for where it all went wrong? The bonkers ending in "28 Years Later" left audiences divided, for one. There was also a very short, roughly six-month gap between installments, which seemingly hurt more than it helped. But playing Monday morning quarterback doesn't help now. It's really about Boyle and co. getting creative to see if they can cobble together the money to bring this story to a close.

#3487. ChatGPT's New GIF Generator Is Fun, but Won't Replace Us Humans (Yet)

Khamosh Pathak is a freelance tech journalist with over 13 years of experience writing online. An accounting graduate, he turned his interest in writing and technology into a career. He holds a specialization in user experience design from ISDI Parsons in Mumbai, where he sought to deepen his understanding of UX, consumer devices, and interplay between software and technology.

Khamosh has written thousands of how-tos and guides on every major platform (iOS, macOS, Android, and Windows). He got started writing how-tos and guides for Guiding Tech, where he also published several e-books. His work has also been seen at MakeUseOf, How-To Geek, and PCMag. He is truly passionate about brewing good coffee.

When it comes to generating AI images, both Gemini and ChatGPT do a passable job. In most cases, the results will look AI-generated, but they likely won’t have glaring spelling issues or missing limbs. Now, OpenAI is trying something new, introducing GIF support for ChatGPT. It's the company's first "moving images" feature since OpenAI shut down Sora, and while you can generate hyper-realistic videos in Gemini, this new ChatGPT feature is trying to fill in the gap, in a small way.

OpenAI is pitching the new feature as an animation tool, not exactly as a way to create looping videos—though that’s how I ended up using it. You give ChatGPT a prompt, as detailed as you can make it, and the chatbot produces a GIF in just a few seconds. You can start with your own drawings or images, too. ChatGPT uses sketches as the base for animations, though it can turn any still image into animated GIFs. Like other AI editing tools, you can edit it if ChatGPT didn't quite get it right: You can ask ChatGPT to make the GIF longer or shorter, remove certain objects, change the style, slow down transitions, among other edits.

AI art can be quite sterile, but I was surprised by how adding motion and animation to the mix makes generating images a lot more fun. Unlike traditional GIFs, which usually pull from existing video clips, you can turn anything you want into a GIF, which is especially cool if you're using your own art. In my testing, I found this to be the most rewarding part. It’s not always possible to one-shot a GIF with a single prompt. But after a few rounds of edits, I ended up creating some GIFs that I actually wanted to share in my WhatsApp groups.

That being said, I think human-made GIFs are still the gold standard here. For example, I asked ChatGPT to generate a video of someone brewing a pour-over, with a gooseneck kettle, showing the coffee blooming process. It did okay, but it’s nothing like actually making a pour-over. The kettle doesn’t move in circles, the water doesn’t rise evenly, there are no bubbles, and the steam is all over the place.

Compare that to the GIF below, which comes from a royalty-free video. Even though it’s a compressed, low-quality, and noisy GIF, it still shows the movement of the pour, the water rising, and even the bubbles. The details captured by a real video just aren’t there in ChatGPT GIFs. If that’s what you’re expecting, you will be disappointed. But I don't think that's the point of this feature anyway.

I found that ChatGPT excels when you’re making something fun, and you don’t look into the details too much. It pulled off a loop of a cat playing with a ball, and it was great at making a festive GIF for Diwali. It even made a GIF based on a photo. I asked it to create a fun promotional GIF for my JBL Bluetooth speakers, and it did the job quite well. At first, the transitions were too jarring, and the movement just made no sense. After some editing, though, I got it to a decent place.

Still, the main issue with ChatGPT GIFs is that complex movement and transitions aren’t nailed down. A hand shifts position weirdly between frames, and colors and objects appear out of nowhere. But if you can get over these issues, you can make some fun, lighthearted GIFs and memes to share with your friends on Instagram or WhatsApp.

#3486. James Bond Director Reveals The Most Important Quality Of Robert Pattinson's 007

Now that Robert Pattinson has officially been cast as James Bond, Amazon MGM's plans for the franchise are coming together. The new owners of the Bond IP are clearly sparing no expense for the upcoming "Bond 26," hiring a major director in Denis Villeneuve to shepherd the project, which will now be led by one of the biggest names in Hollywood. After the missteps that were Daniel Craig's last few films in the tux, it seems Amazon is aiming to re-establish Bond movies as must-see cinematic events. For Villeneuve, however, the star power of his Bond actor is less important than the ability to project the energy of a cold-blooded killer.

In an interview with GQ, the "Dune" director was asked what he looks for in a 007 actor. "A first quality is that I need to believe that this man is a killer," he replied. "Because more than a spy, Bond is an assassin, and I need that kind of strength. I need that kind of anger deep in the eye. It's not everybody who has that." Those who doubt whether Pattinson can do so need only take a glance at the casting announcement video, in which the actor's Bond emerges from the darkness aiming his Walther PPK and wearing a cold, resolute expression on his face. There's a definite edge to his brief appearance in the clip, and you can see why Villeneuve was impressed.

Denis Villeneuve unpacks the process of casting the newest James Bond: Robert Pattinson. https://t.co/DLgqqUErYa pic.twitter.com/FWB1l6r2L8

— GQ Magazine (@GQMagazine) November 17, 2026

That said, it seems Pattinson wasn't actually the first choice for Bond. According to a recent report, Villeneuve initially settled on "Wake Up Dead Man: A Knives Out Mystery" actor Josh O'Connor, who ultimately dropped out and cleared the way for Pattinson. But that will almost certainly prove to be a positive thing.

Robert Pattinson's casting as James Bond breaks a 60-year tradition of the franchise introducing audiences to relative unknowns in the lead role. But that's a good thing, as Bond is in need of revitalization following the debacle that was 2021's "No Time to Die." Pattinson's star power will help restore the franchise's popularity. But the "Batman" star is more than just an A-lister with a built-in audience. He's easily one of the most talented actors of his generation, having demonstrated an extraordinary ability to completely transform on-screen. As Bond, he'll no doubt exude exactly the kind of subtly sinister energy Denis Villeneuve is looking for and which has been one of the most important aspects of the character since his introduction.

In 1962, "Dr. No" kicked off cinema's most enduring franchise by introducing audiences to Sean Connery in the lead role. Rather than casting an established star with the kind of refined energy you'd expect of a gentleman spy, producers Albert R. Broccoli and Harry Saltzman hired a working class former footballer from Scotland, and it was a masterstroke. 007 debuted on the big screen with an edge that only Connery could bring to the role, and that's been an integral aspect of the cinematic incarnation of the character ever since. Sure, director Terence Young helped round off some of Connery's rough edges, but he'd be nothing without the sense of danger the Scotsman brought to the screen. Thankfully, it seems both Villeneuve and Pattinson recognize that, and it's yet another aspect of this casting that bodes well for "Bond 26."

Denis Villeneuve clearly values the killer instinct aspect of James Bond above everything else. But the director has plenty of other requirements for the role. As he went on to tell GQ, "I need someone who has that kind of unapologetic panache, someone that [...] when he comes into the room everything starts to gravitate around him, that kind of strong charisma." It's a foundational aspect of Bond and a characteristic every actor to portray the spy has possessed. But that's not all Villeneuve is looking for.

The French-Canadian filmmaker went on to say he also looks for "sensuality" in his Bond actor, as well as "dark humor" and an ability to take "pleasure into being in deep s***." It's standard stuff for Bond, but it's reassuring to know Villeneuve has such a solid grasp of the fundamentals. Beyond that, the director described someone "strong, muscular, someone that is a force," as well as an individual with a "deep intelligence in the eyes" and who is "always ahead of us." Sounds about right to me. Thankfully, Robert Pattinson can fulfill every one of these requirements, which makes him one of the most exciting of all the James Bond actors.

Thus far, Bond fans have reacted to Pattinson's casting with positivity, even while there's been the predictable objections regarding his "Twilight" years and physicality. At this point, however, the British star has long since proved his ability to deliver consistently electric performances that always surprise. There's no reason to think his Bond portrayal will be any different. Heck, Villeneuve was convinced, and he clearly seems to know what he's talking about.

The 9-1-1 franchise is heating up amid the 2026 TV schedule. While the fall finales of both the Mothership and 9-1-1: Nashville air this week, there's going to be a lot more on the way in the new year. This includes a much-anticipated I Know What You Did Last Summer reunion between Jennifer Love Hewitt and Ryan Phillippe. I'm excited, but what I didn’t expect was Hewitt’s intense take on working with her former co-star again.

Hewitt and Phillippe starred together in the first IKWYDLS film, which was released back in 1997. While Phillippe’s Barry Cox is eventually murdered in the movie, Hewitt’s Julie James becomes the focal point of the sequels. So it’s been close to 30 years since the original movie, and it's great that Barry and Julie are finally back together in some sense.

Following speculation that Phillippe and Hewitt would be reuniting, Hewitt recently confirmed that he would indeed guest star on 9-1-1, reprising his Nashville role as Detective Rogue Kelly. Surprisingly, this is actually the first time that they’ve seen each other since filming wrapped on IKWYDLS, and Hewitt recalled to People just what the atmosphere felt like before the crossover came together. And her take even makes me a bit anxious:

I was so nervous. I had dry mouth and like a full racy heart. Everybody was like, ‘Are you excited?’ I was like, ‘I feel like I’ve forgotten how to act.’ Yeah, it was amazing. We greeted each other with just a big hug and he was like, ‘This is going to be really fun.’ I said, ‘I think it is.’ And it was just, it was a dream.

I love that even though they’ve worked together before, Hewitt can still have those nerves, and I can’t say I blame her. Reuniting with someone you haven’t seen in years -- even if it's on your own turf -- can be intimidating. It sounds like the mood instantly shifted when Phillippe came to set, in a good way, and it makes me even more excited to see how it all turns out.

Phillippe only joined 9-1-1: Nashville for Season 2, so the fact that the two shows are already jumping at the chance to do a crossover featuring him and Hewitt is pretty great. Plus, seeing Phillippe and Hewitt together again is like a '90s-infused dream, and it sounds like they had the time of their lives. Hewitt admitted just how much fun they’ve had from seeing the Internet reacting to the news. She also shared how great it’s been to welcome Phillippe to the 9-1-1 Universe, especially after she reunited with Freddie Prinze Jr. for 2025’s I Know What You Did Last Summer:

He and I have had the best time with people’s reaction. We’ve been DMing going, ‘Did you see it?’ I think we broke the internet. We’ve been having the best time. It was so great because I got to go back and do the movie with Freddie [Prinze Jr.] and sort of have that, and do [our characters] Julie James and Ray again. But this was very different because it was like, [Ryan’s] new in that universe. I’ve been in this universe for a while. It’s such a safe, lovely place to be with the best people. And he and I have not seen each other since I was 18 years old.

As for right now, details surrounding the next 9-1-1 and 9-1-1: Nashville crossover have not been revealed, and I'm eager to see what brings Rogue to Los Angeles. After trying to track down a serial killer in Nashville who is using biblical plagues, hopefully this trip out West will be a bit lighter for him. Of course, if anyone can help him, it’s Hewitt’s Maddie Buckley-Han, who is arguably the best 9-1-1 dispatcher in LA.

Hopefully, crossover information is announced soon, but considering the amount of content Jennifer Love Hewitt has been sharing on her Instagram, she is probably going to keep fans fed for the time being.

For now, viewers can tune in for the fall finales of 9-1-1 and 9-1-1: Nashville, which air this Thursday, November 19, at 8 p.m. ET on ABC, streaming the next day with a Hulu subscription. Both shows will then return from their midseason breaks on Thursday, January 7.

#3484. New camera sensor coming to the iPhone 20 Pro’s main camera, says leaker

The biggest improvement to iPhone photo quality that Apple could make would be to give the device a larger sensor. There have been two reports suggesting this is on the way, although with a potentially rather large catch.

A leaker today says that the iPhone 20 Pro is getting a new and more sophisticated sensor for the main camera, but details are unclear …

There are two main reasons people still buy standalone cameras despite having an iPhone in their pocket wherever they go. The first is lens quality: iPhones have small plastic lenses compared to the far larger and more sophisticated glass lenses used with dedicated cameras.

The second is sensor size. All other things being equal, a larger sensor will capture more light and provide a higher quality image. Current smartphone sensors are absolutely tiny compared to those used in even mid-range consumer cameras.

We’ve seen two previous reports suggesting that a larger sensor is on the way for future iPhones. One of these suggested that it would be coming in 2027 or 2028, although a later one suggested the latter date was more likely.

The reports were not without a catch, however, suggesting that the larger sensor would only be for the telephoto lens and would have a 200MP resolution. Squeezing more pixels into a given sensor size tends to sacrifice low light capabilities in return for higher resolution. This is less likely to be an issue with a telephoto lens, which is normally used outdoors rather than inside.

What I’d really love to see is a significantly larger sensor for the main camera, with no increase in resolution. This would improve low light performance and overall image quality.

A brief report from leaker Ice Universe suggests that the iPhone 20 Pro will get a new and more sophisticated sensor for the main camera.

iPhone 20 Pro to feature a new sensor using 17nm logic process for its main camera next year.

(Under Apple’s current naming system, next year’s iPhone Pro would be the iPhone 19 Pro. However, it’s widely expected that Apple will jump to the iPhone 20 nomenclature in order to mark a significant design upgrade for the 20th anniversary of the device.)

There are no further details, so we don’t know whether the size of the sensor will be increased or remain the same.
